item.title: Fantasy Football Start 'Em, Sit 'Em: Justin Boone's lineup advice for Week 8
item.description: Fantasy football analyst Justin Boone shares his lineup advice for every position.
item.content:encoded:
Make any day feel like Game Day with the Burger King Game Day Menu. Before you take your first bite, get your lineup ready with this week's must-starts and sits.

Justin Boone provides a weekly look at undervalued fantasy players to consider starting this week and potential busts you might want to leave on your bench.

For the rest of your lineup decisions, consult his Week 8 rankings.

Starts

Dak Prescott, QB, Cowboys

vs. Cardinals

Prescott is coming off a three-touchdown game that helped him finish as the QB6 overall last week. It was his first multiple-TD outing since Week 2. 

Now, he faces one of his easiest matchups of the season against a Cardinals defense allowing the third-most fantasy points to quarterbacks, including at least two touchdowns to the last six QBs they've faced. The Cowboys also have the highest implied team total on the week at 30.75, so you can expect another top-half QB1 finish from Prescott. 

Other QBs to start:

  • Jacoby Brissett at Cowboys – On the other side of that game, the Cowboys are giving up the eighth-most fantasy points to quarterbacks. Brissett is always risky, but his last matchup with an easy opponent resulted in a top-10 fantasy finish. I'm expecting something similar this time around. 

  • Kyler Murray at Lions – Murray is still getting comfortable in Kevin O'Connell's offense and a date with the Lions should help. Detroit is the most generous defense to fantasy QBs, with multiple TDs allowed to every quarterback its encountered, including at least three touchdowns to four of those six passers. Murray has also been more productive with his legs lately, which boosts his fantasy floor and ceiling. 

Rachaad White, RB, Commanders

vs. Eagles

Fantasy managers might not realize just how valuable White can be at the moment as a solid RB2 with Jacory Croskey-Merritt on IR. Prior to the Commanders' Week 7 bye, White handled nearly 70% of the snaps, coming away with 57 yards and a score. That's the third time in his last four outings where White has posted either 80-plus yards or a touchdown. While Washington is well rested after a week off, the Eagles — who are already banged up — will be playing on a short week after appearing on Monday Night Football. Philly's once-feared defense has lost its teeth, allowing some huge stat lines over the last month.

With Austin Ekeler and Jeremy McNichols only playing supporting roles, White is positioned to be a top-24 fantasy back in Week 8 and possibly longer.

Other RBs to start:

  • Bhayshul Tuten vs. Colts – Tuten has been remarkably consistent with his yardage totals this season, with at least 87 scrimmage yards in five of his six appearances. Coming off the bye week, Tuten and the Jags are 10-point favorites against a Colts team that just traded away defensive tackle DeForest Buckner and guard Quenton Nelson. Consider Tuten a borderline low-end RB1 this week. 

  • Jordan Mason at Lions – Aaron Jones Sr. returned to practice on Thursday, but it's clear he's not 100% after battling through a knee injury recently. Mason handled 15 carries for 68 yards last week and should see the bulk of the touches yet again. In his only two appearances this year, Mason has racked up 127 yards and a touchdown on 30 carries.  

  • Blake Corum vs. Rams – Corum has found the end zone in three straight games, while putting up at least 60 scrimmage yards in each of those contests. The Rams are 9-point favorites over a Chargers team that's permitting the ninth-most fantasy points to running backs. This is another spot where Corum can deliver top-24 RB production behind Kyren Williams. 

Michael Wilson, WR, Cardinals

at Cowboys

It might seem insane to have Wilson listed as a Start after his disappointing performances the last three weeks since Marvin Harrison Jr. was removed from the picture. Wilson has been the WR52, WR56 and WR24 in weekly scoring, with stat lines of 4-30-0, 4-32-0 and 4-55-0 (with 11 rushing yards). He's also been held to eight targets or less in each of those games, after earning 30 targets the prior two weeks before Harrison's departure.

Now, Wilson gets a shootout with a Cowboys defense that's allowing the sixth-most fantasy points to his position. That makes him a viable fantasy WR2 this week. However, if you have Wilson, you should strongly consider moving him after this performance since he'll face the Seahawks, Rams and Chiefs the following three weeks.

Other WRs to start:

  • DJ Moore vs. Ravens – We've barely seen the DJ Moore experience this season, since he's only taken the field for 60% of the snaps in two contests due to injuries. In those two outings, Moore combined for 18 targets, 11 catches, 167 yards and a touchdown. The upside remains high when healthy, especially in a game tied for the highest projected point total on the week at 54.5.

  • Garrett Wilson vs. Raiders – Fantasy managers are down on Wilson after back-to-back quieter games, but let's not forget he was the WR12 after the first five weeks. Wilson voiced his displeasure with the recent reduced targets on the sideline during last week's loss to the Dolphins and it's setting up a squeaky-wheel situation. The Raiders have allowed double-digit fantasy points to six different receivers over the last month, and I'd expect Wilson to join that list.  

  • Stefon Diggs vs. Eagles – With Terry McLaurin out for the year, the Commanders' receiving corps is going to look a little different coming out of the bye. While Diggs' role might not change that much, he's likely to see more targets. That's notable against an Eagles defense that's giving up the second-most fantasy points to receivers, the sixth-most receiving yards and the ninth-most receiving touchdowns. In the last four games, six WRs have posted at least 70 yards against Philly.

Hunter Henry, TE, Patriots

at Dolphins

Henry has been a streaky fantasy player in the past, so I tend to not get too excited when he puts together three or four strong performances. We're currently in the midst of that kind of stretch with stat lines of 5-62-0, 3-44-1, 4-48-1 and 7-71-0 over the last month. Fortunately, this week he gets a Dolphins defense that's giving up the third-most fantasy points to tight ends. In its last five outings, Miami has allowed at least one touchdown to five different tight ends and the only game during that stretch where it didn't let a TE find the end zone, T.J. Hockenson hit them up for 13 catches and 119 yards. 

Henry is a solid fantasy TE1 once again and even someone you could consider as a flex option this week, especially with A.J. Brown's health concerns. 

Other TEs to start:

  • T.J. Hockenson at Lions – Speaking of Hockenson, he's also a quality start this week against a Lions defense permitting the most fantasy points to tight ends. That includes 10 touchdowns given up to the position in six games. 

  • Brenton Strange vs. Colts – As I mentioned in this week's waiver wire article, Strange is averaging the sixth-most targets among tight ends over the last month and has posted three very usable stat lines of 7-95-0, 7-68-0 and 5-44-0. That includes two top-12 weekly fantasy finishes. Follow that volume into a game versus a spiraling Colts squad. 

Sits

Patrick Mahomes, QB, Chiefs

at Broncos

Mahomes is the featured quarterback to sit for the second straight week after the Seahawks caused him to finish in the single digits for fantasy points. After starting the season with two straight top-10 fantasy results, Mahomes hasn't cracked the QB1 range in his last four games (QB20, QB13, Q23, QB25). 

Injuries to his pass-catchers and offensive line have been part of the problem and are only amplified more in tougher matchups. The Broncos fit that description, especially with Pat Surtain II trending towards a return from his ankle injury. 

It's also worth noting, Mahomes isn't running as much coming off the ACL last season, as expected. After averaging over 30 rushing yards per contest in 2025, he's under 12 yards per game this year. 

Other QBs to sit:

  • Caleb Williams at Seahawks – Williams gets the unenviable draw of facing the Seahawks' stifling defense this week. Seattle has held opposing QBs to the second-fewest passing yards and fantasy points this season.

  • Bo Nix vs. Chiefs – Nix finally had a good fantasy day in Week 7, but it was mostly thanks to a fluky 62-yard TD run. I wouldn't expect much from him against a Chiefs defense giving up the third-fewest fantasy points to QBs, including Nix himself, who only managed 131 passing yards, one TD, one interception and two rushing yards in their Week 1 matchup. 

Omarion Hampton, RB, Chargers

at Rams

Hampton only topped six fantasy points once in the four games before the Chargers' Week 7 bye. We also watched as this backfield became a true three-man, hot-hand committee, with Kimani Vidal and Keaton Mitchell. 

It's possible Mike McDaniel and the coaching staff made adjustments during their time off and are ready to fix the long list of problems with this offense, but expecting that to happen against the Rams is a stretch. 

Sean McVay's crew are 7-point favorites and if the Chargers are trailing, that could limit Hampton's upside, since the routes run were split almost evenly in their last outing (Hampton 15, Vidal 13, Mitchell 12). I'm treating Hampton as a TD-or-bust RB3 until further notice. 

Other RBs to sit:

  • Quinshon Judkins at Steelers – Judkins returned from injury with his best stat line of the season, compiling 104 yards and two touchdowns against the Titans. Those were impressive totals considering he only played 53% of the snaps, while Dylan Sampson handled 46%. Sampson also ran more routes (15-9). It seems likely that Sampson being back will limit Judkins' pass-catching role, which pushes Judkins into more of a TD-or-bust RB3 range in a matchup on the road with a tougher Steelers defense. 

  • Rico Dowdle vs. Browns – Dowdle's 15-touch, 86-yard performance against the Saints needs to be graded on a curve since New Orleans plays a fast-paced style and allows the most fantasy points to RBs. That caused Dowdle's usual 10 touches to inflate to 15. Jaylen Warren remains the clear lead back in Pittsburgh, making Dowdle too volatile to start in fantasy most weeks.

  • J.K. Dobbins vs. Chiefs – In Jonah Coleman's first game off IR, the rookie turned the Broncos backfield into a three-man committee and led the way by playing almost 50% of the snaps. That left Dobbins and RJ Harvey to share the other 50%. Coleman has provided the most juice in his limited action, while Dobbins hasn't been very efficient with his touches. In a difficult matchup with the Chiefs, Dobbins is far too risky to trust in your lineup given the recent trends in Denver's RB usage. 

Rome Odunze, WR, Bears

at Seahawks

Though Odunze is a quality real-life receiver, his role in the Bears' passing attack isn't leading to major fantasy production. After slow starts, Luther Burden III and Colston Loveland have gotten back on track, but Odunze has yet to find the end zone and has only topped 55 yards on two occasions. 

Meanwhile, the Seahawks defense is giving up the fewest fantasy points to receivers and has only let two wideouts top 60 yards against them this season. 

It's always possible Odunze could make a big play and finish with a fine stat line; this just isn't the matchup I want to take a chance on. 

Other WRs to sit:

  • Jaylen Waddle vs. Chiefs – Waddle has been one of the biggest disappointments of the fantasy season and is now dealing with a chest injury. Denver's No. 1 receiver has only gone over 50 yards once in seven games and has just a single touchdown in a Broncos' uniform. This week, he gets to deal with a Chiefs defense that's the second-worst matchup for fantasy WRs and held him to one catch for two yards in the opener. 

  • Xavier Worthy at Broncos – Worthy's big-play ability is always enticing, but as we saw last week, he fades in difficult matchups. The third-year wideout has never posted more than 25 yards against the Broncos and, to make matters worse, Patrick Surtain II is likely returning to the lineup. 

  • Josh Downs at Jaguars – Downs hasn't gone over 50 yards in any of his last four games and is still searching for his first touchdown of 2026. His only hope for future fantasy value would be a trade to a contender. 

Pat Freiermuth, TE, Steelers

vs. Browns

With injuries at the position and four teams on bye — including starting tight ends like George Kittle and Isaiah Likely — it's difficult to recommend sitting any tight end in the top 20. 

Freiermuth earns the mention as a potential sit, since he has yet to reach 50 yards in any game this season. He's also been held to 20 yards or less in three of his last four contests. Freiermuth is always a threat to score a touchdown and he did just that against the Browns back in Week 4. But if you're starting him this week, just know that without a TD, he's likely to let you down. 

Other TEs to sit:

  • Tyler Higbee vs. Chargers – After eclipsing 60 yards in three consecutive games, Higbee has fallen back to earth with stat lines of 4-22-0 and 2-14-0. The Chargers are the ninth-toughest matchup for fantasy tight ends, but that likely won't matter. The Rams will get up in this game and lean on the run. 

  • Mike Gesicki vs. Titans – Gesicki has scored five TDs this season, which has masked some very weak box scores otherwise. In the past two games, Gesicki's only catch in each outing was for a short touchdown. He managed just three targets during that span. That's the most TD-or-bust profile I've ever seen.

item.title: 4 keys to a Lions victory over the Vikings in Week 8
item.description: Predicting what the Detroit Lions will do to earn a victory over the Minnesota Vikings in Week 8 of the 2026 season.
item.content:encoded:
The Detroit Lions (4-2) and Minnesota Vikings (6-0) will meet in Week 8 in an NFC North divisional clash. The Vikings are the last remaining undefeated team in the NFL, and while their defense is playing at an elite level, they’ve yet to face an offense like the Lions, making this a fantastic strength-on-strength showdown.

“Minnesota is playing outstanding football,” Lions coach Dan Campbell said earlier in the week. “(Head coach) Kevin (O’Connell)‘s doing a hell of a job. (Defensive coordinator) Brian (Flores) is doing a hell of a job. This thing, they play very complementary football. […] I’ve got a lot of respect for this team, the way they play, but we’re looking forward to this; this will be good.”

Let’s take a closer look at this matchup and predict how the Lions will earn a victory over the Vikings in this week’s Honolulu Blueprint.

This week’s prediction preview is sponsored by the folks at FanDuel Sportsbook, who currently have the Lions listed at +1800 to win this year’s Super Bowl and are currently 3.5-point favorites in Week 8.

Vikings base scheme

For a detailed look at the opposing scheme, check out our complementary breakdown piece: Lions Week 8 preview: Breaking down the Vikings’ offensive and defensive schemes.

Prediction 1: Counter creativity with creativity

The Vikings enter this game undefeated, but outside of their NFC North games against the Packers and Bears, their opponents have been bottom-of-the-league teams, totaling seven wins and 20 losses combined. Now, they’re headed into the toughest part of their schedule, beginning with the Lions’ elite offense—the first top-10 DVOA offense they’ve faced this season.

The Vikings’ success is built almost entirely on their defense, which ranks in the top 10 in virtually every meaningful defensive statistic and is top one or two in most of them. Over six games, they’ve suffocated teams with their aggressiveness (their 69% blitz rate is over 20% higher than the next-closest team), and with a veteran unit that returns most of its starters, they rarely make mistakes.

I go into more detail in my breakdown of the Vikings defense in the article link above, but at their core, the Vikings are so problematic because of their creative blitzing and quarters zone coverage. On most traditional downs, the Vikings will deploy a base 3-4 defense and line up seven or eight defenders in the box and then “double mug” blitz them, meaning bring an overloaded pressure on a single side of the offensive line or straight up the middle (double A-gap). The goal is to disguise where the blitz will come from and gain an extra blitzer in one area, while unexpectedly dropping players into coverage in the opposite area.

The Vikings are so efficient at disguising their intentions and getting to the quarterback quickly that they lead the NFL in pressures on 49% of pass-rushing attempts, 21 sacks, and a 10% sack rate.

While the Vikings are operating at a scary level, it’s not a defense that is unfamiliar to the Lions and quarterback Jared Goff. In previous seasons, Goff has done well to manage the blitz, especially when he has a healthy offensive line. In games where Goff has succeeded, he’s found creative ways to offset the Vikings’ creativity, and his ability to stay calm under duress—he’s currently the best quarterback in the NFL vs. the blitz, with an EPA of 0.32—has led to success in the six games this season.

Here’s an excerpt from NextGenStats’ game insights:

“Jared Goff has been sacked once and completed 15 of 19 passes for 162 yards and three touchdowns across 20 max blitzes faced this season (i.e., 6 or more pass rushers), resulting in a career-high 78.9% completion percentage. [….] Goff has faced a max blitz on at least six dropbacks in each of his past six meetings with the Vikings during the Brian Flores era dating back to 2023, a threshold he has reached in just three of 51 other games played over that span.”

In recent weeks, purposefully or not, we’ve already seen the Lions testing some concepts to beat an overloaded blitz. Concepts like spreading out five wide, or shifting a tight end into the backfield in a fullback role, will help the Lions offense create quick outlets or adjust their protection. The Lions have also sprinkled in some 21 personnel (two running backs and one tight end), where Sione Vaki stays in to protect, allowing Jahmyr Gibbs to be an outlet for Goff’s passing game.

While the Lions will need to be creative with their running backs and tight ends, their receivers will likely help Goff produce downfield. Last week, we saw the Lions deploy Amon-Ra St. Brown more on the outside, and he caught seven of his nine targets for 109 yards against the Packers. Expect more of that in this game, as the Lions will want to get St. Brown isolated vs. the Vikings’ zone, giving him more space to operate. Also, it wouldn’t be surprising to see them give St. Brown some choice routes, where he can adjust the depth based on who the Vikings blitz.

As NextGenStats also pointed out, the Lions have also found a separation advantage by lining up St.Brown and Jameson Williams on the same side of the formation:

“The Lions’ passing offense has been more explosive when they align to the same side through seven weeks, as they have averaged 8.0 yards per play with a 18.3% explosive-play rate on those snaps.”

By pairing them, Williams can stretch the zone deep and force the defensive backs to adjust to his speed, opening things underneath for St. Brown. If the defense takes the underneath route, then they’ll have to try and stick with Williams one-on-one deep. With the Vikings’ philosophy of limiting explosive plays, look for the Lions to stress their zone and take what they have underneath.

The Lions offense vs. the Vikings defense may be the NFL’s premier matchup this week.

Prediction 2: Pin-and-pull

The Lions won’t be able to rely only on their passing attack in this game; they’ll also need to get their rushing attack going. Detroit tends to lean on its outside zone blocking scheme, but it’ll also need to be creative and unpredictable by incorporating other concepts it’s had success with.

The chart below (adapted from NFL writer Ray Carpenter’s design) shows the EPA from the Lions rushing offense when running in specific directions vs. the Vikings’ EPA in defending those running plays.

No surprise, the Lions are finding most of their rushing success behind left tackle Penei Sewell, and it lines up with where the Vikings have been weakest. But the Lions won’t simply want to run behind their All-Pro all game; they’ll need to get creative too.

With the Vikings lining up so many defenders on the line of scrimmage, the Lions will want to attack those edges, and the pin-and-pull concept can cool off some of Minnesota’s aggressiveness. Let’s look at the final offensive play from the Packers game to see an ideal example of the Lions deploying a pin-and-pull concept to get outside leverage and open a massive rushing lane for Jahmyr Gibbs.

On this third-and-6 play, the Lions run a toss-left to Gibbs with the tight end (Sam LaPorta) and wide receiver (Isaac TeSlaa) cracking down (“pin”) on the Packers’ two outside edge players. In concert with the “pin,” the Lions “pull” Sewell and left guard Christian Mahogany under and outside left to get out in front of Gibbs. Additionally, the Lions put St. Brown in motion, and he seals the opposite edge of the hole by blocking the corner. Here’s the pre-snap look with the blocking assignments in red:

And now the results after the snap with the “pin” circled and the pull in solid red arrows:

Prediction 3: Put Vikings offense behind the sticks

While the Vikings defense has played lights out, the offense has struggled. Despite being billed as “the answer to the Vikings deep ball problem,” quarterback Kyler Murray has been anything but.

Heading into this game, the Vikings offense ranks 30th in DVOA; Murray is throwing for 162.3 yards per game (29th), and the team ranks 25th in explosive plays. Murray’s average depth of target (ADOT) is 7.13 (30th), and his Aar yards to sticks (how close to the first-down marker he targets his passes) is -2.97 yards, 37th among quarterbacks with at least 50 passes this season.

Most of their drives fizzle out quickly—they average 0.259 first downs per play, last in the NFL—because they throw short and rely on their skill players to gain yardage. The issue is that defenses have caught on and are shrinking the box, preventing the Vikings’ skill players from gaining yards after the catch (YAC)—they have 519 YAC this season, 31st in the NFL—which often puts the Vikings offense behind the sticks.

As a result, the Vikings don’t typically have sustained drives, and through six games, they’ve had the fewest trips to the red zone in the NFL — just 13 trips (for reference, the Lions have 27)—and scored just four offensive touchdowns in the last four games combined.

Look for the Lions to follow suit with the Vikings’ previous opponents, shrink the workable area for the offense, take away the intermediate area of the field, and make their tackles when Murray throws short—currently, the Lions lead the NFL in missed tackle rate (9.0%) and fewest missed tackle yards allowed (153).

If the Lions can find early down success and get the Vikings behind the sticks, they’ll get off the field.

Prediction 4: This is the game to unleash the blitz

One way the Lions can find early down success against the Vikings offense is to utilize the blitz.

The Vikings offensive line has done well in pass protection this season, allowing only 65 pressures (fourth best) through six games and averaging a 32.7% pressure rate (11th best). However, despite the few pressures allowed, the sacks have come easier; Vikings quarterbacks have been sacked 18 times this year (ninth most) at a 9.9% rate (third highest). Teams have recognized this pattern and blitzed Minnesota 36.3% of passing plays, the seventh highest rate this season.

Lions edge rusher Aidan Hutchinson is moved around the defensive line, but he lines up across from the right tackle on most plays, meaning he is expected to square off with Vikings Brian O’Neill. Over his career, Hutchinson has a 15% pressure rate vs. O’Neill (slightly above his career average of 13.9%), but the Vikings, like most teams, will likely give O’Neill help by double-teaming or chipping Hutchinson. If the Vikings dedicate extra attention to Hutchinson, it will open up opportunities for the other defensive linemen, and if the Lions want to crank up the aggression, there is value in sending an extra defender and pressuring Murray.

This is another way for the Lions to put the Vikings offense in an early hole, get them behind the sticks, and the Lions offense back on the field.

item.title: Saints Draft Position: NFL Week 8
item.description: Two great options for the Saints in 2027
item.content:encoded:
The New Orleans Saints lost another game, and sadly, it really didn’t change much in the draft order. Like these past two seasons, the bad teams keep losing, and it’s keeping the Saints away from a single-digit pick, so in the bye week, the Saints are set to select at pick 10 in the NFL Draft. 

Here are some players the Saints could select at 10.

OG Greg Johnson 

Looking at top guard options, Greg Johnson is the guy in the first round, although 10 may be a little bit of a reach, guard is becoming more and more important in today’s NFL, and the Saints need a starting RG. If they do not move on from Cesar Ruiz before the deadline, it’s going to happen in the offseason. Although I do like Jeremiah Wright, there’s no reason to believe he can start next season, and I don’t want the Saints to rely on that to happen. 

The other caveat to this selection is the coaching staff. If Kellen Moore, this coaching staff, and the front office are still in place, I don’t want the Saints to make this selection. They have good offensive linemen that are regressing under them already, so I wouldn’t expect a rookie offensive lineman to have much success. However, it’s the perfect selection for a new coaching staff and GM who hopefully knows the trenches, and a new head coach who can elevate this rookie. 

DL Xavier Gilliam

The caveat put in place for the Johnson pick should be here as well. The Saints haven’t done well lately at drafting defensive linemen. Doesn’t matter if it’s a defensive tackle or edge rusher, it doesn’t work out. So, if a new staff is put in place, Xavier Gilliam would be a really good option. 

He is incredibly athletic, extremely quick off the snap, can win against offensive linemen with power and different pass-rush moves, and is equally dominant against the run. Gilliam is a player you will see throughout any game blowing up plays in the backfield, but he also makes the right decisions and has a consistent impact when he’s not creating incredible moments. The Saints do not have a DT anywhere close to the player Gilliam is on their roster, and putting him next to Chase Young could really elevate this entire defense.

item.title: Trade for QB Justin Herbert? Browns fans split; have strong reaction to the idea
item.description: If Justin Herbert trade rumors start for the Chargers, Browns fans are split on the idea of adding the struggling QB
item.content:encoded:
When it comes to surprises so far in the 2026 NFL season, the Cleveland Browns 5-2 record, sitting atop the AFC North, is among the biggest. There are others, including the Minnesota Vikings being the lone undefeated team and the Los Angeles Chargers being the lone winless squad, but the Browns success in Year 1 under HC Todd Monken has been fun for Cleveland fans and an interesting storyline for the NFL as a whole.

A win in Week 8 would change things greatly for the Browns chances of turning “surprise” into “NFL playoff participants.”

Cleveland’s success has come with five come-from-behind wins, with QB Deshaun Watson regaining a version of his elite past late in both halves of games. The rest of the time, the Browns have seen inconsistent play at the quarterback position. That, along with Watson heading into free agency after the season, leaves questions about the future of the position.

Enter QB Justin Herbert and the winless Chargers:

So, we asked Browns fans the same question and, so far, they are split almost right down the middle:

A quick look at Herbert’s season shows why the idea of trading him is even being discussed publicly at all:

  • 59% completion percentage
  • 5 touchdowns
  • 8 interceptions – Which leads the NFL
  • Career-worst yards per attempt and significantly worst adjusted yards gained per pass attempt (2 strong QB metrics)
  • Passer rating of 68.8 and QBR of 29.3 – By far his career worsts
  • Chargers are 0-6

So, a lot of reasons for Los Angeles to potentially look to trade what was assumed to be their franchise quarterback and lots of reasons for Cleveland fans to be hesitant (or stronger words) about trading for him:

As seen in the poll, not everyone was against the idea:

A couple of our loyal readers brought up interesting points. First, dawngregry brought some straight facts followed by some opinions on where a trade might land:

Then, Spidey mentioned a big variable: Would the Browns be gunshy to pull the trigger on another big QB deal after the Watson failed deal?

In the end, a Herbert trade seems highly unlikely for a variety of reasons, including his no-trade clause. Cleveland also seems unlikely to upset the apple cart as they’ll head into the NFL trade deadline with a winning record, at worst, and potentially a commanding lead in the AFC North. Most likely, if Herbert were to be traded, the 2027 NFL offseason would be the earliest, when the Chargers could figure out what their future holds.

For now, Browns fans are almost exactly split on the idea of trading for the struggling superstar, but the poll still has a little bit of time to change drastically. So, vote in the poll and join the conversation in the comment sections.

item.title: NFL predictions: Browns-Steelers square off in meaningful midseason match-up for once
item.description: Can the Browns complete the season sweep of Pittsburgh?
item.content:encoded:
This Sunday, the Cleveland Browns (5-2) take on the Pittsburgh Steelers (5-2). Below, we analyze a few advantages, disadvantages, or general thoughts about the two teams before getting to our predictions for the game.

It’s Been 23 Years

If I could put the meme from the Titanic here, I would, with respect to it having been 23 years (which is a 22-game losing streak) since the Cleveland Browns have won a road game against the Pittsburgh Steelers in the regular season. We’ll always have that playoff victory over them, but we’re trying to keep focused on the unfathomable statistic of losing 22 in a row somewhere.

Of course, the reason for that has largely been that the Browns have been a bad football team, while Pittsburgh has generally been good. But, it’s not like Cleveland hasn’t been able to beat Pittsburgh during that stretch at all. In fact, at home since 2003, the Browns are 10-13-1, including winning 7 of their last 8 games there. On the road, they are 1-22, with 22 straight losses.

That 2003 match-up was one featuring Tim Couch as the Browns’ starting quarterback, as he went 20-of-25 for 208 yards, 2 TD, 1 INT, and 1 rushing TD in a 33-13 victory. Cleveland still have the classic quartet of Kevin Johnson, Quincy Morgan, Andre’ Davis, and Dennis Northcutt as their receivers, with Steve Heiden as their primary tight end. William Green ran 33 times for 115 yards. Pittsburgh was led by Tommy Maddox at quarterback, with Amos Zereoue and Jerome Bettis running and Hines Ward, Plaxico Burress, and Antwaan Randle El as their receivers. Phil Dawson was putting kicks through the uprights for the Browns. I was 14 years old back then, just starting high school. I’m 37 now, having been through college, had a full-time job for awhile, and started a family. It’s time we turned the corner for the Browns, isn’t it?

Home-away records sometimes seem less valuable these days. I could go into context and say that Cleveland’s 2-2 road record this year was the team just not being prepared in Week 1, and also because of sloppy rain conditions against the Jets, and not because ‘they weren’t at home.’ But when you just look at the records straight up, the Browns are 3-0 at home. Also 3-0 at home this year? The Pittsburgh Steelers, with wins over the Falcons, Bengals, and Colts. They, like Cleveland, have had a relatively soft schedule this year, but it’s let them build some confidence and work out some things too. This game won’t be easy, but I’m excited for it.

Those Darn Slow Starts

Last week, I harped on the Browns needing to get their offense rocking, especially with KC Concepcion, and also needed the defense to stop allowing opening-drive scores. Cleveland accomplished half of that with the offense taking off, but the defense found themselves in a 14-0 hole before getting things back on track. Thinking back to the first Steelers game, Pittsburgh began the game with a 17-play, 73-yard drive that took up 9:48 of game clock. Then, until the fourth quarter, their drives were: interception, punt, missed field goal, field goal, punt, punt, and punt.

It’s always been a known factor in the NFL that some teams can have greater success on their first drive with well-scripted sequences. But it’s a bit mind-blowing that this defense can play so well the rest of the game — which I’ve attributed to Mike Rutenburg’s ability to make adjustments — but they can’t get that stop, even out of dumb luck, on the first drive.

I know Rutenburg would say that it doesn’t matter if that touchdown drive comes on the opening drive, or the fifth drive, they want to stop it. But setting the tone early will be a factor as some of these games get more serious. The last time these teams played, Cleveland erupted for 21 straight points in the second quarter. That isn’t going to happen every week (even though they erupted for 17 points in a row just last week, after being in a hole…)

Here are some other notes:

  • The running game was encouraging last week. I like some of the little things we’re seeing improve with team blocking, and I also like the adjustment to go under center more. I think Cleveland, in their efforts to make Deshaun Watson comfortable, have often gone from Shotgun, which can hurt the running game at times. Watson has been much more unphased this year, and I think we’re seeing how being under center can add some things to the ground game, quick passing game, and even springing someone like KC Concepcion open off of playaction.
  • Speaking of Concepcion, the usage of him last week was picture perfect. Keep doing it — he is the one guy who can really propel this offense to the next level, and help open things up for other guys too. The number of crossing routes that Cleveland has started taking advantage of is perfect too.
  • Jaylen Warren is the guy who the Browns need to stop. He’s averaging 5.5 yards per carry on the season, and with the return of Rico Dowdle last week, the duo has been very effective on the ground.
  • I still fear Darnell Washington to a degree. The big tight end had a touchdown catch against the Browns, and has a touchdown catch in each of the past two games. I’d be tempted to put Emmanuel McNeil-Warren on him at times to see what happens.
  • The big X-Factor this week that could throw a wrench in Cleveland’s chances is the fact that Tytus Howard might be out with a concussion. That would put Dawand Jones in as the starting right tackle. We all remember back in 2023, when Jones — in limited action — ‘shut down’ T.J. Watt, which got everyone excited about Jones’ future. It’s been a bit rough since then, and with injuries and lesser playing time, Jones hasn’t looked very sharp during fill-in duty.
  • And then what happens if Jones goes down with an injury? I’m assuming that KT Leveston will be a gameday elevation from the practice squad, but remember, he was outright cut after being a contender for the starting right guard job in camp. Cleveland drafted Austin Barber to be a reserve offensive tackle, but he’s flourished at right guard. I suppose the they could shift Barber to right tackle, Elgton Jenkins to right guard, and then put Luke Wypler at center. On paper, that works for me. However, with the continuity these guys have built up, would they want to switch three linemen as opposed to just one? Fingers crossed that Jones not only stays healthy, but plays has a solid outing.
  • According to FanDuel, the Browns are 3.5 point underdogs against the Steelers. The over/under is 39.5.

Quick Hitters

Offensive coordinator Travis Switzer was asked about if the running game so a breakthrough this past week, but he just appreciated the collective effort and improvements on first and second down:

“Yeah, I mean, I think a lot of the things, we have been seeing improvement over the last couple weeks, so it was great to see the production that we had on Sunday. As far as breakthrough, I don’t know. I don’t know that any of our guys really look at it that way. I think that the things that we’ve been emphasizing to improve, we’ve been. We were a lot better on first and second down, which allowed us to get more runs called. You know, the more you’re on schedule, the more you’ll be able to run the ball. So, as far as breakthrough, I don’t know. I mean, we were certainly really happy to see the production that we did, and we’ll continue to try to improve.”

Defensive coordinator Mike Rutenberg wouldn’t really give an answer to the slow start of the defense each week, other than they treat every drive the same as far as diagnosing what went wrong behind closed doors:

In everything we do, when it is to our collective standard, we are constantly trying to get it better. So, whether it’s the first drive, something else, something we’re doing really well, it’s a constant under construction through the week of why, tell the truth, try and figure it out together and fight our a—- off really to fix it. And it’s a really cool process, collectively, as a staff and players.”

Special teams coordinator Bryon Storer was asked about a couple strategic elements, and I’m going to post two quotes from him this week, because I appreciate the insight. The first was what happened on the 12-men penalty on the punt that led to a Titans first down, and then later, he talked about the two touchbacks by Andre Szmyt to start the game:

“Absolutely. [Monken] got every right to be angry about that situation, and that ultimately falls on my shoulders, 100%. So, I take full responsibility for the 12 men on the field. I’ve got to catch that. So, the situation was, it was fourth-and-one. And in a fourth-and-one situation, we don’t usually go with our normal punt return team. It’s our safe team, as they like to say it, and it’s majority of defensive players, all defensive players on the field. So, in that situation, you’re thinking about fake the whole time. And going into the game, we are very ‘fake’ aware that there could potentially be a fake run against us. So, in all honesty, we had the safe team out there, and one of our punt return players stayed on the field. We were so fake aware in that moment, we failed to notice that there was 12 men on the field. And so, it just cannot happen. It’s a big-time learning lesson for me as a coach. And then we addressed it with the guys, we instituted a few different fail-safes to make sure that never happens again, because that absolutely cannot happen again moving forward.”

…

“So, we’re going to kick it to him. And so, but I did tell Dre (Andre Szmyt) he could be a little bit more aggressive, because we’d rather have it more towards the goal line versus being caught on the five-to-10-yard line and have him have a full head of steam with basically one cut. So, I told him, ‘hey, you can be more aggressive toward the goal line.’ After the first one, I said, hey, Dre, no big deal. You know, we’ll get him the next one. And then the second time I was a little bit more disappointed. Said, Dre, we can’t do that twice now. So, our whole philosophy going into that game was to cover kicks, and so we would rather not kick touchbacks in those situations.”

Here are predictions from multiple staff members at DBN:

Predictions

Chris Pokorny: “Cleveland has lived and died with close games for much of the season, so why should this one be any different? The Browns’ defense was effective against Rodgers and company for much of that game, even though he came one yard away from the 300-yard mark. The Browns need to play a clean game, but I think the positive momentum continues, as this unit has shown that they are unphased by the big moments.” Browns 23, Steelers 20

Jared Mueller: “There are only two ways I see this game going, and I’m going to pick the one I don’t want to see.

The Browns are either going to blow the Steelers out by 10 or more points, or lose a close one to a veteran-laden team on the road. It feels like a game Cleveland can control, if they can get out of the blocks early and avoid penalties, with Pittsburgh coming off last week’s game in Paris. A couple of mistakes, and Aaron Rodgers taking advantage of the Browns aggressive defense could change the game for the Steelers.

Let’s hope I’m wrong.” Steelers 20, Browns 18

Thomas Moore: “It has been 23 years of blowouts, close calls, and general nonsense whenever the Browns travel to Pittsburgh. HC Todd Monken is not concerned about any of that and the message should filter down to the players.

There is no logic applied here – which makes sense since a 23-year losing streak is completely illogical – so the Browns are going to continue to embrace their “do whatever you have to do and pull it out at the end” style of play.” Browns 17, Steelers 10

Barry Shuck: “Just not seeing it. The Browns are 0-10 in the last decade in Pittsburgh. But they did win that playoff tilt in 2020. I believe the Browns will split with everyone in their division, just not on the road. Steelers have a very good run defense, which means Deshaun will need to fling it all day. Stats show when QBs throw for the average of 28 times a game, there is a chance of winning. But those contests when the QB has to air it out 40-50 times, it means the run game is crappy, and a lose is inevitable.” Steelers 27, Browns 13

Ezweav: “Literally everything points to another disappointing day over there at Ketchup Field.  The history in particular is just so daunting, our worst game every year is over there, and we’ve all been through this time and time again.

But these players and coaches aren’t the same guys.  They have not bought in AT ALL to the sad-sack ‘woah is me’ attitude so many previous teams (and a lot of current fans) bring into this contest.  To them, this is a team they kinda pushed around a month ago, winning narrowly a game they really should have won comfortably.  There’s nothing actually all that special about the Steelers at this point.  They’re old, we’re not.

So against all better judgement (specious though that may be in my case) we’re going all in.” Browns 25, Steelers 13

item.title: Giants trade deadline: Titans’ RB might be a good Plan B for New York
item.description: Let’s discuss an alternative to Jonathan Taylor if the Giants want to add a running back.
item.content:encoded:
The New York Giants appear to be targeting running back and defensive tackle help at the 2026 NFL trade deadline.

The top two defensive tackles, DeForest Buckner and Jeffrey Simmons, are already off the board. So, the Giants will likely have to look for more incremental, short-term help there.

The top running back, and probably the biggest fish remaining in the trade market pool, is Jonathan Taylor of the Indianapolis Colts. Taylor doesn’t sound like a player who wants to be traded, and the price might be prohibitive for a team like the Giants that is not in a championship window.

So, when it comes to running backs, where should the Giants turn for an upgrade?

Potential trade target: RB Tony Pollard

If the Giants want to upgrade their running back room and a Taylor trade isn’t going to happen, the view here is that Pollard should be the next target.

Why it would work

Pollard is not the bell-cow back that Taylor is, and he would not give John Harbaugh the “Derrick Henry or Saquon Barkley circumstance” he would like to have. He would, though, give Harbaugh an upgrade over Tyrone Tracy and Devin Singletary to team with Cam Skattebo in a two-headed timeshare.

Pollard, 29, has never averaged fewer than 4.0 yards per carry in eight seasons since being a fourth-round selection by the Dallas Cowboys in the 2019 NFL Draft. He is currently averaging 4.3 yards per carry for the Tennessee Titans and is on pace for a career-best 1,171 rushing yards, which would be his fifth consecutive 1,000-yard season.

Pollard is also a useful receiver, having caught at least 30 passes in each of the last five seasons.

Pollard is in the final year of a three-year, $21.75 million contract with the Titans. The Giants would only be responsible for the prorated portion of his $6.74 million 2026 base salary. Over 10 weeks, that would be $3.74 million.

Why it wouldn’t work

The 1-6 Titans are terrible. It would seem to make sense for them to get something in return for a 29-year-old running back who is likely headed to free agency at season’s end. Maybe, though, it doesn’t.

As bad as they are, the Titans are still trying to develop 2025 No. 1 overall pick Cam Ward into an effective NFL quarterback. That is not going well. Trading away their best running back and more or less neutering their run game isn’t going to help their young quarterback.

If the Giants make a bid for Pollard, they would likely want the cost to involve one of the two sixth-round picks they have in 2027, or a fifth- or sixth-round pick in 2028. With the potential to create a bidding war, and the idea of supporting Ward for the remainder of the season, the Titans could hold out for better picks. Or, not trade Pollard. The only currently tradeable mid-round pick the Giants have in 2027 is a third-rounder. They have no fourth-rounder (traded for Malachi Fields) and no fifth-rounder (traded for J.J. McCarthy).

The locker room might be another factor. We saw how tight-knit the running back group of Skattebo, Tracy, and Singletary is at the end of the victory over the Houston Texans. I don’t believe the potential for disrupting that chemistry would prevent the Giants from making a trade for Pollard, but it is something they should consider.

item.title: Panthers fire defensive coordinator Ejiro Evero after 3-4 start
item.description: Evero was hired in 2023 under former coach Frank Reich and remained in the role when Dave Canales was hired.
item.content:encoded:
Carolina Panthers defensive coordinator Ejiro Evero and defensive passing game coordinator Jonathan Cooley have been fired, the team announced on Thursday.

The moves come a day after the Panthers fell to 3-4 after a 27-19 loss to the Green Bay Packers.

Evero had been in charge of the Carolina defense since being hired in February of 2023 to work under then-head coach Frank Reich. After remaining in the role when Dave Canales replaced Reich, Evero signed a contract extension through the 2027 season this past January.

The Panthers defense has allowed 349.6 yards per game this year compared to 327.2 in 2025. Carolina has also allowed the seventh-most points this season (27.6) compared to the 22.4 last season. They have also recorded the fifth-fewest sacks (11) in the NFL.

Cooley joined the Panthers in 2023 as a cornerback/secondary coach before taking over the passing game coordinator job a season later.

Defensive line coach Todd Wash will take over as interim defensive coordinator. He joined the Panthers in 2023 after two seasons as the Detroit Lions' defensive line coach. Wash will be assisted by outside linebackers coach/run game specialist AC Carter, who will also oversee the defensive line.

Despite the 3-4 record, the Panthers remain tied with the Atlanta Falcons atop the NFC South.

item.title: Eagles Film Preview: Philadelphia’s passing plan must punish the Commanders’ blitz
item.description: Analyzing Philadelphia’s Week 8 matchup from an All-22 perspective.
item.content:encoded:
Each week, I’ll publish two film-room previews: one focusing on the offense and one on the defense. These are primarily film-based, focusing on the schemes, tendencies, and matchups that could shape Sunday’s game, with all statistics coming from the Fantasy Points Data Suite. I also record a video version for Patreon, where I break down the plays in greater detail and where you can further support my work.

I think the Commanders’ defense is a little better than its numbers suggest. The secondary has some talent, and Daronte Jones can create problems with his pressure packages. However, the lack of a reliable four-man pass rush is killing this defense. For the Eagles, this matchup comes down to whether they can handle the blitz. If they can, there should be opportunities to score.

Pass Defense

The Commanders are allowing around +0.15 EPA per dropback, ranking 26th, but I don’t think that tells the whole story of their secondary. Looking at the individuals, there is more talent here than those results suggest. The problem is getting everyone to play the same coverage correctly while asking them to hold up for too long.

Moving to a new system has brought some predictable communication issues. Some plays each week show defenders with different understandings of how a route should be handled. The red-zone example below looks like Cover 4, but the two sides don’t seem to be operating with the same rules. The underneath defender carries a route on one side, while the cornerback on the other passes a receiver off to nobody.

Those are the opportunities the Eagles need to create and exploit. Motion, changes in formation and route combinations that force defenders to exchange responsibilities should be part of the plan. There are capable coverage players here, but making them communicate and adjust gives you a chance to expose the mistakes. If you just line up and throw isolation routes, I’m not sure the Eagles are good enough to win.

Jones comes from the Brian Flores school of defensive football, and you can see the influence in the disguises and unusual pressure looks. Sometimes it’s fascinating. Sometimes I think they are asking their players to do too much.

The Tampa 2 disguise below is a good example. A cornerback follows the receiver across the formation, suggesting man coverage, before the defense rotates into zone. I like that part! However, Frankie Luvu is lined up over the A gap and then has to become the deep middle defender. That is an enormous amount of ground to cover, especially for someone whose best work comes moving toward the quarterback.

The disguise is supposed to make the quarterback hesitate, but it can also create a difficult assignment for your own defender. The Eagles need to read the movement after the snap and attack the space before that defender can get there. Tanner McKee will have to distinguish the initial picture from the coverage they actually play.

The biggest issue, though, is the pass rush. They simply don’t generate enough pressure with four. The Commanders blitz on 47.4% of dropbacks, the second-highest rate in the league, yet their overall pressure rate is only 34.4%, ranked 18th. That is a lot of extra rushers for a fairly ordinary amount of disruption.

The individual numbers reinforce the film. Odafe Oweh and K’Lavon Chaisson are the main edge threats, but neither has consistently taken over games by winning his matchup. Daron Payne contributes pressure inside, but this isn’t a front that reliably wrecks the pocket without help. When the initial rush stalls, quarterbacks have time to wait for routes to develop and find the gaps between defenders.

That is why I’m reluctant to blame all the passing production on the secondary. There are coverage mistakes, but there are also snaps when the coverage has done enough, and the quarterback is still standing comfortably in the pocket.

I do think Quan Martin is a weak link when playing deep. His recognition of crossing routes needs to be better, and he can be slow to react and affect the throw. There are opportunities to manipulate his positioning and attack the space around him.

Mike Sainristil has also had a terrible season, but his role has changed. With Trey Amos back, Sainristil played only seven defensive snaps in their last game. The Eagles shouldn’t expect the same opportunities to target him that they had in Week 1. Amos, Rasul Douglas, and Amik Robertson give this secondary a more credible group of corners, and Douglas and Robertson have both shown plenty of good individual coverage.

The Commanders play a lot of two-high coverage, particularly Cover 2 and Cover 4. Their two-high rate is 69.6%, second highest in the league, and they are predominantly a zone defense. That doesn’t mean the Eagles should abandon the idea of throwing vertically. There are opportunities downfield.

The classic Cover 2 hole shot, between the cornerback and the safety along the sideline, has been available. Posts and Go routes have also produced high-value plays against them. The Eagles need to recognize the coverage and take those chances when protection allows.

Again, the pass rush is a huge part of the explanation. In the example below, the Commanders send five, and the quarterback still gets a beautiful pocket. You can debate the spacing in the secondary, but at some point somebody up front has to make the quarterback uncomfortable.

This defense is at its best when it blitzes. Extra pressure gives them a better chance to disrupt the play before the coverage is stretched. If I were in the Commanders’ defensive meeting this week, I would plan to blitz the hell out of the Eagles. I would make this offense prove it can identify the pressure and consistently get the ball to the right place. Given the Eagles’ problems answering pressure this season, I would be stunned if the Commanders didn’t lean heavily into that approach. I think we see a 50%+ blitz rate. This will not be like the Cowboys game.

Expect overloads and defenders dropping from unexpected places. An edge defender showing rush can become an underneath coverage player, while a linebacker or defensive back replaces him. The offensive line, quarterback, and receivers need to understand the same answer. Getting the protection right is only part of the job if nobody is available for McKee to throw to.

I want quick options that give McKee somewhere to go immediately when the defense brings more than the protection can handle. Empty can also help clarify the picture and spread the pressure threats out, as long as the ball comes out on time. The Eagles can’t keep responding to pressure by reducing the route options and hoping the remaining receivers eventually get open.

One player I would be particularly careful around in the middle is Sonny Styles. Everyone gets excited watching Frankie Luvu blitz, but Styles is the defender who really caught my attention in coverage. His range is outstanding for a linebacker, and he already shows an impressive understanding of the routes developing around him.

He can threaten pressure near the line, recover into coverage, and get underneath a throw that initially looks available. He isn’t simply dropping to a landmark and waiting. He can relate to the receiver, recognize the next threat, and close a window. Some of it is ridiculous for a rookie. It really helps this defense.

If the Eagles want to attack the middle, I would rather make Luvu defend those routes. He can be drawn toward an underneath receiver, leaving room for a deeper crosser behind him. Dallas Goedert could have opportunities there, but McKee needs to know where Styles is before releasing the ball. A window that looks open at first may not stay open for long.

Run Defense

Their run defense is stronger than the headline EPA ranking suggests. They rank 20th in EPA allowed per rush, which makes this look like another defense the Eagles should run through. However, opposing running backs have managed only 465 yards on 121 carries, averaging 3.84 yards per carry. That is solid conventional run defense.

Daron Payne is a major reason why. He is an outstanding run defender who can make it difficult to create movement inside. Their heavier fronts also cover interior blockers and restrict the combinations an offensive line wants to use. The Eagles will have to earn their yards rather than assume that a two-high look automatically gives them an easy running opportunity.

Kinlaw’s knee injury is worth monitoring because losing him would affect that interior rotation. But even if he is unavailable, I wouldn’t suddenly treat this as a soft run defense.

The biggest reason the overall rushing figures look worse is quarterback scrambles. They have allowed 132 yards on 17 scrambles, with those plays producing +1.102 EPA per attempt and an 88% success rate. That is a significant problem, but it isn’t one the Eagles can exploit in the same way with McKee. It also connects to their pass rush. If the pressure loses its lanes and the underneath defenders have dropped into coverage, a mobile quarterback can escape into space.

There are still ways to attack their conventional run defense. I saw plenty of cutback opportunities when defenders overran the initial direction of the play. Whoever is starting at running back needs to recognize when there is room to cutback. Their aggression can work against them when they lose control of their fits.

Inside zone looks more promising than repeatedly trying to stretch this defense with outside zone. They have allowed 5.53 yards per carry on inside zone runs, compared with 3.36 yards per carry on outside zone runs. For the Eagles, I would build on the more direct running concepts that looked better against the Cowboys and look for those cutbacks, rather than going back to outside zone.

Styles’ range doesn’t mean he always finishes. He misses a lot of tackles and isn’t as good against the run as he is in pass coverage. The Eagles can earn yards if they get their backs into space, but getting through the front is the hard part.

Final Thoughts

I don’t think this is a particularly good defense overall, but I do think it is better than a quick look at the passing and rushing rankings suggests. The corners are more credible with Amos back but the four-man rush is the weakness that keeps putting the rest of the unit in difficult situations.

The Commanders’ game plan should be obvious to predict. They will bring pressure repeatedly and make the Eagles solve it. That is where this matchup will be decided. If McKee gets clear answers, the protection handles the exchanges, and the receivers are available quickly, the Eagles should be fine. There are downfield opportunities when they get a clean pocket, and the defense’s disguises can leave space to attack.

The Eagles need a passing plan that punishes the blitz. They showed some offensive improvement last week, but this is a different test. Make the Commanders pay for bringing extra rushers, and force them back toward the four-man rush that has let them down all season.

Thank you for reading! I’d love to hear your thoughts, so feel free to comment below and ask any questions.If you would like to support me further, please check out my Patreon here!

item.title: Raiders-Jets Week 8: 5 things to watch
item.description: Keys to victory at New York
item.content:encoded:
The 3-4 Las Vegas Raiders play at the 2-5 New York Jets on Sunday. Kickoff is at 10 a.m. PT. Here are five keys to victory for Las Vegas:

Stop the run:

The Rams ran right over the Raiders as they compiled 199 yards on the ground last week. That is a recipe for a defeat. Rob Leonard’s unit must tighten the ship this week.

Run the ball:

Yes, this has been a focal point every week and every week it seems to be a problem area for Las Vegas. The Raiders have had the worst running game in the NFL this season. Last week, they ran the ball just 17 times. They have to establish the run at some point. Ashton Jeanty said he think the Raiders can run on the Jets because they have some players not interested in tackling. It’s time to live up to those words.

Be Better in red zone on both sides of the ball:

On offense, in the past two games, the Raiders converted in the red zone just three of 10 attempts. On defense, in the past two games, the Raiders allowed touchdowns on eight of their opponents’ 10 trips to the red zone. That’s another recipe for defeat. That must change this week.

Be better than a bad team:

The Raiders are 3-0 against teams with a combined record of 3-16. They are 0-4 against teams with a combined record of 17-9 record. The Jets are 2-5. The Raiders are better than the Jets. They need to show it.

Take advantage of an Aaron Glenn weakness:

Since he took over in 2025, Jets head coach Aaron Glenn’s team have been outscored 106-7 in the final two minutes of the first half. That’s a weird quirk. But it’s real. Go take advantage, Las Vegas.

The Los Angeles Rams will make their running game a major priority once again when they meet the Chargers in Sunday’s Battle of Los Angeles. Expect Sean McVay to lean on his backfield early and often, using Week 7’s blueprint to control the tempo, wear down the Chargers’ defense and open up opportunities in the passing game. The Rams have found a successful formula by establishing the run, and there is little reason to abandon it against their cross-town rivals. Sunday’s matchup could produce another big day on the ground, with Los Angeles committing to the run regardless of how effective its passing attack might be early. Here are several predictions for what should be an intriguing divisional-style showdown between two Los Angeles rivals.

1. Rams score on opening drive touchdown

Los Angeles’s offense has not been pretty with scoring on its opening drives in 2026. The Rams drives this year…

Week 1 vs. SF – Punt (3 plays)

Week 2 vs. NYG – Punt (3 plays)

Week 3 @ DEN – Punt (7 plays)

The Rams not only get points, but a touchdown on the opening drive.

2. Joshua Karty is elevated to game day roster…for kickoffs

With Karty’s signing to the practice squad and Brandon McManus being on the 53 man roster, Los Angeles is clearly eyeing Karty for its kickoff role. If the Rams are saying yes to Karty on kickoffs, I’ll be curious to see who is made inactive on gameday to give way for the team to have two kickers on the active gameday roster.

3. Rams generate five 20+ yard plays on offensee

Whether its through the running game or passing game or a combination of both, the Rams will find a way to get more explosives going on Sunday. Puka Nacua is always a safe bet to catch 1 or 2 explosives. Blake Corum has shown ability to hit the running hole and take off. I think LA’s offense finds balance with its running and passing explosives.

4. Rams run the ball 30+ times for second consecutive week

The Rams finally found their running game in Week 7 when they gave Kyren Williams and Blake Corum a combined 33 rushing attempts. Both players nearly went for 100 rushing yards/each. With both players providing significantly weekly contribution, Coach McVay has to stick with the recipe that made Los Angeles play its best game in 2026. I see the two getting another 15+ attempts again…

5. Tutu Atwell catches 50+ yard pass

With the Rams beginning to have an identity towards the running game and short passing game (checkdowns to running backs), opposing defenses may be inclined to bring their secondary closer to the line of scrimmage. The caveat is that Tutu Atwell is fast. And McVay will be looking for the opportunity to dial it up deep.

item.title: Matt LaFleur explains Packers’ offensive line decisions
item.description: Another game with more surprises up front.
item.content:encoded:
Another week, another new offensive line configuration in Green Bay. This time, the Packers had three different starters than in their last game, featuring new or different faces at all three interior line spots.

Aaron Banks made his long-awaited (or, perhaps, long-feared, depending on your opinion of Banks) return to his left guard spot, finding his way into the lineup for the first time since he played 22 snaps in Week 2.

Laken Tomlinson flipped from left guard to right guard, making his first start on the right side since the Obama administration.

And John Williams made his first ever NFL start at the position he played where he played game snaps for the first time ever last week.

But, you know, other than that it was basically a normal week up front.

Why this configuration, though? John Williams at center makes logical sense; he played there last week and is the only remaining player the Packers seem to like at the spot with Jacob Monk on injured reserve, although Jager Burton may end up there eventually. But at the guard spots, Matt LaFleur offered little explanation for the moves he made.

“Well I just think when you look at it, you know, the way Laken’s been playing, you can’t take him out of the lineup. And I thought Aaron Banks coming back…so we went with that route,” he said postgame.  “That’s not to take anything away from [Kevin] Zeitler. Certainly we feel good about him as well. But we thought that was the move.”

There’s plenty to unpack there, assuming LaFleur is being completely forthright (and that’s a big assumption, given he has no incentive to shoot straight with us).

First, LaFleur asserts Tomlinson has been playing well. “Playing well” might be a bridge too far for me, but he’s at least better than Donovan Jennings, Jager Burton, and Jacob Monk, so I’ll concede the point. He’s at least been okay in pass protection (and LaFleur praised the Packers’ pass protection later in his postgame remarks). 

Second, LaFleur seems to take it as a matter of course that Banks deserves to be in the lineup. But Banks was active last week and didn’t play. Travis Glover started at right guard and Tomlinson was at his familiar left guard spot. The lineup math there would seem to indicate LaFleur thinks Banks is worse than Glover and better than Zeitler (who was inactive against the Lions). 

And what of Zeitler? The Packers signed him to a one-year, $4.05 million deal on September 30, but he hasn’t been on the field for a single snap on offense so far, though he’s played 15 snaps on special teams. His contract includes heavy playing time incentives and he stands to reap some not-inconsiderable financial rewards if he hits certain playing time thresholds, but it’s hard to believe the Packers would really be pinching pennies that hard. So what gives? Is he not in game shape? Is he really not better than Tomlinson or Banks (or Glover, for that matter)? It’s a mystery, and LaFleur didn’t give us any significant explanations after the Packers’ Thursday night win.

In fact,he muddied the waters even further, pointing out when asked that Tomlinson was not getting regular reps at right guard before the Packers installed him there this week.

“It’s definitely a challenge and he answered the bell,” LaFleur offered of Tomlinson’s sudden appearance on the right.

That may be so, but it appears to be a challenge of the Packers’ own making. But that describes a lot of their offensive line issues this year, for what it’s worth. Until the Packers can get out of their own way, it seems doubtful the offensive line will improve much more.

The Jets are unlikely to have one of their top young defensive players when they host the Raiders on Sunday.

Head coach Aaron Glenn told reporters in his Friday press conference that edge rusher David Bailey will not practice on Friday and is doubtful for the game.

Bailey is dealing with a groin injury and has not practiced this week.

The No. 2 overall pick of this year’s draft, Bailey has registered 5.5 sacks, seven tackles for loss, and nine QB hits so far this season. He also has three forced fumbles.

Running back Breece Hall (quad) will once again be limited in practice on Friday and is questionable for Sunday’s game. He has been limited in practice all week.

Offensive lineman Dylan Parham (knee) will also be questionable.

Defensive lineman T’Vondre Sweat (knee) has been ruled out.

item.title: Week 8 Fantasy Football Matchups to Exploit: 5 players you should have in your lineup
item.description: Ray Garvin takes you through five players in smash spots for fantasy football in Week 8.
item.content:encoded:
It's Week 8 of the fantasy football season and Yahoo analyst Ray Garvin is back to give you five players with matchups they can exploit on Sunday.

Blake Corum, RB, Rams vs. Chargers

I think we're getting to the point where we have to start taking Blake Corum seriously as a weekly fantasy option.

Listen, Kyren Williams isn't going anywhere. He's still a very good running back and an important part of what the Rams want to do offensively. But what Corum is doing right now cannot be ignored.

Last week against Las Vegas, Corum carried the ball 17 times for 93 yards and a touchdown. He played 44.4% of the offensive snaps and actually finished with one more rushing attempt than Williams. Over the past two games, Corum has accounted for approximately 45% of the Rams' rushing attempts.

That's not some backup coming in to spell the starter for a few snaps. That's a legitimate role in this offense.

And when you watch Corum, he's running with confidence. He's decisive, he's physical and he's making the most of the opportunities he's getting. With Davante Adams unavailable, I expect Sean McVay to continue leaning on his running backs to move the football.

There's also the ball-security conversation with Williams, who lost another fumble against the Raiders. I'm not suggesting Corum is about to take over this backfield, but when you're playing well and the guy ahead of you is putting the ball on the ground, that certainly doesn't hurt your case for additional opportunities.

Now Corum gets a Chargers defense allowing 4.24 yards per carry to opposing running backs, and the Rams have done an excellent job creating running lanes.

Corum doesn't need to take Williams' job to be valuable in fantasy. He's already getting enough work to matter. If the Rams continue splitting opportunities the way they have recently, Corum is firmly in the flex conversation with legitimate upside this week.

Bucky Irving, RB, Bucs vs. Falcons

This is what we've been waiting to see from Bucky Irving.

Twenty-four carries, 106 rushing yards and two touchdowns against Carolina last week. That's the type of performance fantasy managers envisioned when they drafted Bucky, and what's encouraging to me is that the workload was already trending in the right direction.

He had 21 touches against Pittsburgh the week before, but the production wasn't there. We finally saw the opportunity translate into fantasy points against Carolina.

And I think there's a good chance that continues this week against Atlanta.

The Buccaneers rank fourth in adjusted run-blocking yards per carry, while the Falcons rank 23rd in that metric allowed. That's a favorable matchup for an offensive line that has been creating opportunities on the ground.

We just watched Christian McCaffrey put up 100 scrimmage yards and a touchdown against this Falcons defense. Now, Bucky isn't McCaffrey, especially in terms of the receiving role, but the point remains: you can run the football against Atlanta.

There are a few things worth monitoring. Bucs RT Luke Goedeke is dealing with a calf injury, Kenny Gainwell has a hip injury and Baker Mayfield's recovery from a dislocated right thumb remains something to watch. Those situations could affect the offensive environment, but I'm not building this recommendation around anybody missing the game.

I'm looking at Bucky's workload, how he's running the football and the matchup in front of him.

If Irving is going to continue getting 20-plus opportunities, he's the type of running back I want in my lineup. The volume is there, Tampa Bay is blocking well and Atlanta presents another favorable opportunity.

I'm rolling with Bucky again this week.

Parker Washington, WR, Jaguars vs. Colts

I continue to believe Parker Washington is one of the more interesting wide receivers in fantasy football right now, and coming out of Jacksonville's bye week, I love the matchup against Indianapolis.

He's emerged as Trevor Lawrence's primary receiving option, commanding approximately 26% of the targets when he's on the field. That's significant usage for a player who still doesn't get discussed nearly enough in fantasy circles.

And this matchup sets up really well for him.

The Colts play man coverage on nearly half of their defensive snaps. Against man coverage this season, Washington has averaged 0.66 PPR points per route run. That's outstanding efficiency, and it's exactly the type of matchup advantage we should be looking for when setting our lineups.

Indianapolis also just traded DeForest Buckner, removing one of its most established defensive linemen. That's a significant loss for the Colts and should make things easier for Lawrence and the Jacksonville offense.

I also like RB Bhayshul Tuten in this matchup. I think Jacksonville should be able to have success running the football, especially with Buckner no longer anchoring that defensive front.

But here's the thing: both can be successful.

Washington doesn't need Jacksonville to completely abandon the running game to produce. He's established himself as a featured part of this passing attack, and with the Jaguars getting an opportunity to reset during their bye after the London trip, I expect this offense to come out ready to go.

The one concern is overall passing volume if Jacksonville gets out to a big lead. But I'm not going to overthink a player commanding this type of target share against a defense that plays as much man coverage as Indianapolis.

Washington has the usage, the efficiency and the matchup. That's the combination we're looking for.

Garrett Wilson, WR, Jets vs. Raiders

Man, these past couple of weeks have been frustrating if you're a Garrett Wilson manager.

And honestly, it's felt like the Omar Cooper Jr. show.

Cooper has put together back-to-back 100-yard performances, going for 103 yards against New England and 115 against Miami. Meanwhile, Wilson has caught just six passes for 70 yards combined over those same two games.

That's not what fantasy managers signed up for.

But I'm not ready to throw in the towel on Wilson, and I actually think this matchup against Las Vegas presents a great opportunity for him to get back on track.

Two weeks ago, Wilson was dealing with Christian Gonzalez, one of the better cornerbacks in football. Last week against Miami, the production simply wasn't there, and Cooper continued to establish himself as a legitimate weapon in this offense.

I'm not taking anything away from Cooper. He's earned his opportunities. But that doesn't mean Wilson suddenly forgot how to play wide receiver.

This week, the projected matchup against Hezekiah Masses is one I believe the Jets can exploit. Masses is allowing approximately 0.34 PPR points per coverage route, and while receivers aren't locked into one matchup for an entire game, this is an area New York should be looking to attack.

The Raiders also play a significant amount of zone coverage, so Wilson will have opportunities to find space in different areas of the field.

Look, I understand the frustration. When you're setting your fantasy lineup and looking at what Wilson has done over the past two weeks, it's difficult to feel confident. But we've got to separate recent production from the opportunity ahead.

Wilson is too talented for me to completely abandon him after two disappointing games, especially in a matchup like this.

Cooper can continue to play well without Wilson disappearing from this offense. I think there's room for both receivers to produce, and I'm willing to bet on a bounce-back performance from Garrett this week.

Michael Wilson, WR, Cardinals at Cowboys

If there's one player on this list who has probably tested the patience of fantasy managers more than anybody else, it might be Michael Wilson.

When Marvin Harrison Jr. was traded, the expectation was that Wilson would step into a significantly larger role in Arizona's offense and deliver consistent fantasy production.

The opportunity has been there. The results? Not so much.

But this is where I think we have to be careful about allowing recent fantasy performances to dictate every lineup decision.

Because this matchup against Dallas is about as good as it gets.

First, look at the game environment. We're talking about a game with a 54.5-point total. The Cowboys have an offense capable of putting points on the board, and that could force Arizona into a game where it has to throw the football to keep up.

That's exactly the type of situation I want for a wide receiver who needs opportunities.

And we've seen what opposing receivers can do against this Dallas secondary. Makai Lemon just had success against the Cowboys on Monday night, and there's no reason to believe Arizona can't create opportunities for Wilson as well.

But here's the number that really stands out to me. Wilson is averaging approximately 17.4 expected PPR points per game, yet he's producing only 11.5 actual PPR points.

That's nearly six fantasy points per game separating his opportunity from his actual production.

Now, expected fantasy points don't guarantee future production. We know that. But they do tell us something about the opportunities a player is getting, and Wilson's usage suggests he should be delivering more than what we've seen.

That's why I'm not ready to give up on him.

I want Arizona taking shots downfield. I want Wilson getting opportunities in scoring position, and against this Cowboys defense, I believe those chances will be there.

At some point, you've got to trust the process and the opportunity.

If you're not willing to start Wilson against the Cowboys in a game with a 54.5-point total, what matchup are you waiting for?

This is exactly the type of spot where I'm willing to go right back to him.
