item.title: Panthers fire DC Ejiro Evero; name interim DC and defensive play caller
item.description: The Panthers have shaken up their defensive staff after the Thursday Night Football loss to the Packers in Week 8.
item.content:encoded:
The Panthers took an ugly 27-19 loss to the Packers on Thursday Night Football, and Carolina responded to that loss by parting ways with defensive coordinator Ejiro Evero and defensive passing game coordinator Jonathan Cooley.

Todd Wash was named interim defensive coordinator and will call the defensive plays, according to a release from the Panthers shared by Joe Person of The Athletic.

Ejiro was hired by the Panthers as the team’s defensive coordinator in 2023 after one season in the DC role with the Los Angeles Rams. He was hired during Frank Reich’s tenure as the Panthers’ head coach, but Dave Canales retained him when he was hired by Carolina.

Wash spent five seasons as the Jaguars’ defensive coordinator. From the Panthers’ release:

Wash originally joined Carolina’s staff in 2023 and has 31 years of coaching experience, including 20 in the NFL. He spent five seasons (2016-20) serving as the defensive coordinator for the Jacksonville Jaguars, including in 2017 when the team had the second-ranked defense in the league and advanced to the AFC Championship Game.

It wasn’t just Thursday night’s loss that led to the decision. The loss to the Packers on a short week came on the heels of an embarrassing 43-13 loss to the Buccaneers in Week 7. But Baker Mayfield only threw for about 63 yards, and the Buccaneers ran all over Carolina. On Thursday night, the Panthers let Jordan Love throw for 288 yards and three touchdowns while Bryce Young took six sacks and finished with a QBR of 36.2.

In addition to the termination of Evero and Cooley, the Panthers announced that OLB/run game specialist AC Carter will also take on defensive line coaching responsibilities. Secondary coach Renardo Hill will retain his position.

The Panthers are sitting at 3-4 and remain in first place in a very weird NFC South, but if the Falcons win this week, that will change. If you’ve paid any attention to the Atlanta Falcons, you know that’s always a big “if.”

We will update this story as more information becomes available.

item.title: Panthers fire DC Ejiro Evero, name Todd Wash interim in defensive shakeup
item.description: The Panthers are making changes to the defensive coaching staff. Carolina has fired DC Ejiro Evero and named Todd Wash as the interim.
item.content:encoded:
The Carolina Panthers have fired their defensive coordinator, Ejiro Evero, the team announced on Friday, Oct. 30.

Along with Evero, Carolina also parted ways with defensive passing game coordinator Jonathan Cooley. The defensive line coach, Todd Wash, has been named the interim defensive coordinator and will handle the play-calling duties on that side of the ball.

As part of the changes, outside linebackers coach and run game specialist AC Carter will now also coach the defensive line. Renaldo Hill, the secondary coach, will continue in his role.

The moves come not even 12 hours after the Panthers lost to the Green Bay Packers on "Thursday Night Football."

Evero was hired as the Panthers' DC in 2023 under then-head coach, Frank Reich. He was retained when Dave Canales took the job in 2026.

Why did the Panthers fire Ejiro Evero?

The Panthers' struggles on defense all season long were enough for the team to part with Evero.

Carolina is allowing the sixth-most points per game (27.6) and the third-most rushing yards per game (140.7) in what has been a season-long issue. After allowing the Tampa Bay Buccaneers to score 43 points in a Week 7 blowout loss, Carolina followed that up with a 27-19 loss on "Thursday Night Football" in Green Bay.

With 10 days to prepare for their next game, the timing made sense for the Panthers to make a move.

And while injuries have been an issue, not meeting expectations is a bigger one. The Panthers are coming off an NFC South division title in 2025 and nearly knocked off the Los Angeles Rams in the wild-card round. No one was planning a parade for an 8-9 team that snuck into the postseason, but the idea was that Carolina could build off that.

Instead, Canales' team is 3-4 after seven games in what is a winnable NFC South. Despite the under .500 record, the Panthers are still in first place.

Making the move now allows the team a chance to right the ship defensively, as best it can, while making a playoff push.

Who is Todd Wash?

Wash began his coaching career at the college level in 1996, serving as defensive coordinator for NCAA Division II Fort Lewis. He made the leap to the NFL in 2007 as a defensive quality control coach for the Buccaneers.

The 58-year-old has bounced around the league with the Seattle Seahawks, Jacksonville Jaguars and Detroit Lions before joining the Panthers coaching staff in 2023.

This wouldn't be the first time that Wash has been a defensive coordinator at the professional level. That was the position he held with the Jaguars from 2016 to 2020. His tenure also included the second-ranked defense in the league in 2017 when Jacksonville advanced to the AFC Championship Game.

item.title: These 4 NFL teams need to stop lying to themselves — it'll be better for fantasy football if they do
item.description: Fantasy football analyst Chris Allen examines four teams that should consider a change ahead of the NFL Trade Deadline.
item.content:encoded:
I've been slowly setting up a workshop in my garage. The workbench is a folding table. The miter saw sits on a pair of sawhorses. Every project needs a workaround, and I tell myself it's fine. But after improvising the same cut a third time, "I can make this work" turns into "I'm buying the right tool."

A few NFL front offices have to be having that same talk right now.

"The run game isn't broken."

"The WR room isn't empty."

But the patchwork fixes aren't holding, and the trade deadline is coming on Nov. 10. If nothing changes, some of these teams should be shopping.

That matters for us, too. Every move an NFL team makes reshapes the fantasy football value of the players already on the roster. So, let's look at the situations that need a change and the players those teams should target.

The Bengals Should Make Their Strength Stronger

The trade-deadline talk around Cincinnati's offense will center on the run game, specifically whether the Bengals should go get Jonathan Taylor. To be clear, I don't disagree. A new (better?) element would keep my favorite team's playcalling fresh and give it more answers against good defenses. But after watching the Bengals dominate Baltimore, I think they already have a solution.

pic.twitter.com/IQemgcUJ7I

— Performances (@NotPerformances) October 25, 2026

Joe Burrow blacked out in the second half. His PROE shot up to +12.8%, played one snap under center and proceeded to confuse every defender in a purple jersey. Between the high pass rate and quick throws (2.48 sec avg time to throw), shades of the 2024 season started peeking out. That's especially true when looking at who's on the other end of his throws.

  • 2024: 42.8% (Chase/Higgins Target Rate), 58.5% (Chase/Higgins Air Yard Share)

  • 2026: 44.4%, 70.7%

The league's best WR duo coming into the season has been that through seven games. Burrow's thrown 82 first downs. No. 1 and No. 5 account for 45 of them. Burrow's 15 TDs? Chase has five and Higgins has two. There isn't a Burrow stat that doesn't pull the current WR12 and WR14 in half-PPR scoring into the limelight. However, their gravity isn't just pulling defenders toward them; it's keeping the ball from everyone else.

  • Dohnte Meyers: 49.2% (Route Rate), 20 (Total Targets), 7.8% (1D per Route Run)

  • Mitchell Tinsley: 32.5%, 8, 7.5%

Cincinnati used 11-personnel groupings on 56.9% of their offensive plays, its second-highest rate of the season. And yet, Meyers and Tinsley are forgotten aspects of the rotation. Meanwhile, the pass-catchers around them continue to get hurt.

TEs Erick All Jr. and Tanner Hudson are out for the season. Higgins and Chase got hurt against Jacksonville, and Chase's new ankle injury bears monitoring. As has been the case since 2020, this offense flows through Burrow's arm. But the best version has been with the ancillary options working in concert with the Big 3. Tennessee just moved on from its best defender in Jeffery Simmons, which should give Burrow more time to work in the pocket. If we're still not seeing anything from the second-string receivers, I'd rather the Bengals add a wrinkle to their aerial attack than focus anywhere else on the offense.

Mahomes Needs A Guy

As I mentioned earlier in the week, hindsight being 20/20, the Chiefs should've added a receiver during their bye week. Or at least start cycling through guys on the practice squad. It's like the Colts' reliance on Alec Pierce for the passing game to function. I didn't know Tyquan Thornton, who only caught 19 passes in the same offense last year, would be so critical to their '26 plans. But looking back at Week 7, it's hard not to come to the same conclusion.

FUMBLE!

Derick Hall forces it for Seattle but the Chiefs recover.

KCvsSEA on NBC/Peacock
Stream on @NFLPluspic.twitter.com/8COtXd1IEQ

— NFL (@NFL) October 26, 2026

Pause the video at two seconds. Check out where all of the KC pass-catchers are in relation to Seattle's defenders. It wouldn't have mattered if Mahomes stayed in the pocket for two seconds or two minutes (well, all right, maybe two minutes). His receivers weren't gaining separation. Of course, I'll cop to over-emphasizing a single play. But when you zoom out on the games before and after the bye, the need for new blood stands out.

  • EPA per Dropback (on throws to WRs): 0.21 (Weeks 1-4), -0.26 (Weeks 6-7)

  • Passing aDOT: 10.7, 6.6

  • YAC per Completion: 6.2, 5.0

I know I have WRs specified in the metrics, but I wanted to single out KC's top-two pass-catchers: Travis Kelce and Xavier Worthy. Both are below the 50th percentile in ESPN's Open Score. Accordingly, Mahomes is throwing shorter, getting less out of those attempts and his efficiency plummets as a result. 

Sunday's divisional rematch against the Broncos is the ideal test for the Chiefs offense. Since Week 1, Kyren Williams is the only RB to gain more than 75 yards on the ground against them. They'll need more than the "Kenneth Walker III, go do cool stuff" plays this time around. But if we don't see more routes and targets for Cyrus Allen or shots on timing routes to Jalen Royals, we should expect to see a new face in the WR room before the trade deadline.

Vikings Should Take the Pressure Off Kyler

If I'm Minnesota's coaching staff, here's how I'm thinking about facing the Lions. Detroit plays fast (fourth-most plays per game, fifth-fastest time in between plays), and the Lions know how to score (second-most PPG). Slowing things down and reducing possessions would be my formula. DC Brian Flores can solve part of the equation with his hair-on-fire defense. But the other side of the ball is a variable.

Kyler Murray All 22 vs Colts
14/24 150 yards 1 TD

Underwhelming performance by Kyler Murray and the offense overall. He made some very good accurate throws and always missed on some easy ones. We will need him to get better as we approach the half way point of the season.… pic.twitter.com/XZJpv33AEE

— KD (@GamedaySpotLite) October 29, 2026

Now, remember — I said variable, not bad. However, if the margin for error against a team like the Lions is already thin, some level of certainty would be great. But for Kyler Murray, it's been one step forward and then one step back.

  • Week 3: -3.9% (CPOE), 18.8% (Passing Success Rate)

  • Week 4: +7.6%, 39.0%

  • Week 5: +11.8%, 48.4%

  • Week 7: -7.5%, 40.7%

Murray has faced obvious passing situations on 32 dropbacks since coming back to the lineup. He's attempted 24 passes. Only three have resulted in a first down. Yes, he's used his legs on the remaining eight snaps, and half of those have converted. For the mathematically inclined, that's a 21.9% conversion rate. But you don't need to have any skill with numbers to see how Murray's inefficiency has affected his receivers.

Justin Jefferson is averaging 61.5 YPG, and Jordan Addison's 57% catchable target rate ranks 49th out of 66 qualifiers (min. 100 routes). T.J. Hockenson has been the only bright spot out of the pass-catching corps due to his 6.8-yard aDOT. If Minnesota wants to keep the clock ticking, they'll need more than hoping Murray has everything under control. But a boost from the running game would be nice, too.

Aaron Jones Sr. is managing a knee injury, with Jordan Mason (likely) in line to assume the RB1 role. Sure, Mason getting more volume is a boon for fantasy. But we played this game last year. In Weeks 3-7, while Jones was out, Mason averaged 15 carries per game. He had two games with zero targets. Three of his four outings resulted in less than 60 yards. The opportunities didn't turn into points, and we're headed into a similar situation in Week 8.

Now, the offensive line is better. Plus, Detroit has allowed two 100-yard rushers. Simply put, the environment is conducive to Mason not only keeping the offense on schedule, but creeping into the fantasy top 12, too. However, if he struggles, forcing Murray to try and shoulder the load on his own, the rumors of Minnesota adding another RB may turn into a reality.

Praying for a Backfield in NOLA

Don't worry. I know the Saints are 2-5 and dead last in their division. However, remember, it's the NFC South. New Orleans is one win behind the leader. Plus, its schedule, relative to the rest of its division mates, opens up. However, if it's going to make a playoff push, a repeat of its trip to Paris can't happen again.

42-year-old Aaron Rodgers had more rushing yards (8) than ANY Saints player today…

Tyler Shough: 8 YDS
Kendre Miller: 6 YDS
Alvin Kamara: 5 YDS pic.twitter.com/DjhQfXvcCD

— BET99 Canada (@BET99CA) October 25, 2026

Getting out-gained on the ground by a 42-year-old man is, well, it's something. Typically, you'd expect to see Tyler Shough make something happen on his own. The Saints' QB1 ranks 11th in touches (24). But an injury to his non-throwing hand has limited his output. Before facing Atlanta, he was averaging 22.3 YPG on the ground. Since then, he's down to 13 YPG. It hasn't stopped him from trying, though. But without Travis Etienne Jr. leading the backfield, Shough's efforts haven't helped.

  • Early-Down Rushing Success Rate (since Week 4): 32.9%, 31st 

  • Explosive Play Rate: 2.7%, 29th 

  • Average Distance to the Sticks on Third Down: 8.8, 26th 

Shough has dropped back to throw in a third-and-long situation 30 times throughout his last four games. That's the third-most of any starter. He's converted on 17.9% of those throws. That's the sixth-lowest rate of any starter. And he hasn't gotten much help from the guys behind Etienne.

  • Kendre Miller (on Early Downs): 52.5% (Stuff Rate), 19.0% (Rushing Success Rate)

  • Alvin Kamara: 57.1%, 8.3%

  • CJ Donaldson: 50.0%, 0.0%

By most metrics, the Saints' run blocking has been league average. They're 13th in run-block win rate, but their composite PFF run-blocking grade has them at 25th. But the trio of backup RBs has been met at or behind the LOS on over half of their early-down totes.

New Orleans may be on its bye, but we're already getting rumors about Jordyn Tyson coming back. However, we're yet to get a similar update about Etienne. If the rest of the NFC South continues to stay in a state of disarray, the Saints could capitalize on the situation by adding to their rushing attack.

item.title: How the Vikings Can Neutralize Jahmyr Gibbs and Upset Detroit
item.description: Vikings plan to exploit Jahmyr Gibbs, trade deadline buzz, and Flores' defensive "opus"—all on The Real Forno Show.
item.content:encoded:
How can the Minnesota Vikings beat the Detroit Lions? Simple—exploit Jahmyr Gibbs. On the latest episode of The Real Forno Show, host Tyler Forness and producer Dave Stefano broke down the Vikings’ key to victory, a wild NFC North trade ahead of the deadline, and why Brian Flores’ defense could be the ultimate difference-maker on Sunday.

The show opened with blockbuster news: the Chicago Bears acquired DT Jeffrey Simmons from the Tennessee Titans for two first-round picks and a fourth. Forness questioned the fit within Dennis Allen’s read-and-react scheme: “If Simmons comes in and it’s just Jeffrey Simmons, it’s not gonna matter that much.” The Bears still lack edge rushers, raising questions about whether the move translates. Meanwhile, the Vikings have been reportedly aggressive in the run up to the deadline, with names like Maxx Crosby and Jalen Carter circulating. “If you bring in Jalen Carter, that’s become the centerpiece of your defense,” Forness said. “That is the guy that you are building everything around.” He emphasized that such a move wouldn’t be for 2026 alone—it would be a long-term foundational piece, especially with Andrew Van Ginkel and Kyle Van Noy hitting free agency. Forness was blunt on the quarterback front: only Daniel Jones and Kirk Cousins, both familiar with Kevin O’Connell’s system, make sense as trade targets. “You’re not trading for great players at this point. You’re trading for somebody who you hope can steer the ship.” On J.J. McCarthy’s departure, he added: “He got himself traded. The Vikings didn’t do it because they wanted to give up on him. He earned it.”

The heart of the episode centered on neutralizing Gibbs in pass protection. Last Christmas, the Vikings forced Gibbs into a career-high 15 pass-protection snaps—over 35% of his total—resulting in seven pressures and a sack. “They made it so Gibbs was basically ineffective because of their blitzing and how they attacked,” Forness explained. With Van Ginkel, Blake Cashman, Ivan Pace Jr., and Dallas Turner matching up on him, the plan is straightforward: make Gibbs block, or take him off the field entirely. Stefano noted the broader impact: “By having him pass block, he’s not out in their patterns either.” Flores’ defense, refined over three seasons, has reached what Forness called his “opus” and a “pile driver onto a steel chair.” Stefano captured the confidence: “Our defense does. They know what they’re doing. The question is, how quickly can Goff figure it out? And I don’t think anybody’s figured it out this season.” Forness agreed: “I do think that this defense is good enough to win a Super Bowl on their own.”

Key Points:

  • Gibbs exploitation: Vikings will blitz in the 70–85% range, forcing Gibbs to pass-protect or leave the field
  • Flores’ finalized defense: Three years of refinement into a system nobody has solved
  • Trade deadline: Maxx Crosby and Jalen Carter as long-term defensive cornerstones; Daniel Jones as affordable QB insurance
  • McCarthy’s exit: Talent was never the question—”He got himself traded”
  • Offensive key: Kyler Murray must “take a deep breath, play more relaxed, and trust Justin Jefferson and Jordan Addison”
  • Lions’ defensive weakness: 30th in EPA per play, 31st in explosive play percentage allowed
  • Prediction: Vikings favored by 3–3.5; Forness picks Minnesota: “I think they’re gonna be able to take down Goff”

item.title: Christian Watson’s WWE-style ambulance return made for the best internet edits
item.description: Christian Watson went to the hospital during Thursday Night Football, then made a Stone Cold-style return.
item.content:encoded:
There is a saying around these SB Nation parts, as well as in the wider sports media space, that holds the following:

Everything is pro wrestling.

Say what you want about the WWE, the AEW, and pro wrestling at any level, but you can draw comparisons between what happens in the squared circle and almost every aspect of public life. I mean, the current President of the United States is a member of the WWE Hall of Fame, but that is a discussion best left to another time.

But Thursday night’s game between the Green Bay Packers and the Carolina Panthers gave us perhaps the best WWE-NFL comparison yet.

Packers wide receiver Christian Watson left the game — and the stadium — following a catch on a deep ball in the first half. Watson was described as having a chest injury, and not only was he checked out in the blue medical tent, but he departed Lambeau Field via an ambulance for further evaluation.

Shortly after halftime, however, Watson was back at Lambeau Field, having been cleared by the medical staff at a nearby hospital. He returned in the same ambulance, this time riding up front, and jogged back onto the field to a loud “pop” from the Packers faithful:

The comparisons to pro wrestling were immediate:

That prompted some to overlay the video with audio from WWE matches, like this video here:

Or this video:

It is worth mentioning that Watson was diagnosed with a broken rib and was coughing up blood, but he indeed returned to the game and caught two more passes as the Packers defeated the Panthers. The wide receiver finished the game with a career-high eight catches for 113 yards, the highest receiving yardage total from a Packers player this year.

But just how close of a comparison was this, really, to the WWE?

Watson drew the comparison in his post-game comments:

item.title: Commanders GM Adam Peters talks NFL trade deadline, Antonio Williams and more
item.description: Commanders GM Adam Peters conducted his weekly interview with 106.7-FM and detailed several key topics off the bye week
item.content:encoded:
The Colts dealt superstar guard Quenton Nelson to the Seattle Seahawks earlier this week. 

The Commanders did not make a play for him.  

Washington general manager Adam Peters was clear about that in his weekly (paid) interview with 106.7-FM The Fan on Friday morning. He addressed the NFL trade deadline and several other topics during the interview, including receiver Antonio Williams, cornerback Amik Robertson and the state of the Commanders coming out of their bye week.  

Also, Peters revealed that receiver Terry McLaurin is having Friday surgery to repair a torn patellar tendon.

Here are the highlights from that interview – the full session can be found below – as Washington steamrolls into a vital Sunday night matchup with the Philadelphia Eagles.  

On the NFL trade deadline 

We’re looking at everything. Any position on our team where we can make our team better for the present of the future, we’re always going to look into that. Whether it’s wide receiver of any other position that you can think of, we’re going to look for us to get better. There aren’t a lot of opportunities to do this. There are times where teams are looking to move on from guys you’re interested in and those are opportunities where you can make a move.  

On Antonio Williams 

First and foremost, I want to give a shout out to Terry. He’s having surgery today. For all those who do so, please say a prayer for him. He’s a big part of what we’re doing and what we’ve done. I just want to send him some love here today. Moving forward with Antonio, every single day he does something special in practice that shows you what kind of talent he has, what kind of instinct he has as a receiver. The sky’s the limit for him. With Terry going down, that creates more opportunities for others and people will have to step up. We’re still hoping and expecting that Antonio will do that. He’s definitely capable of that.  

On the Amik Robertson and his guarantee 

We went out and signed Amik for a reason, because he’s a straight dawg. He’s a very good player. He has the utmost confidence and has an edge and an attitude and impacts a defense. I love that he’s on our team. Listen, that’s the mindset you want. For sure that’s bulletin board material if you do subscribe to that, but I’ve always said that, if you need bulletin board material to get ready for a division game on Sunday night, then – all the material and motivation – that’s kind of a problem, you know? 

On Chig Okonkwo 

We’ve high hopes for him. He had a slow start because he got hurt, and now we’re seeing what that’s going to look like within our offense. We really haven’t seen the full extent of what he can do within our offense in terms of catching and running. We’re going to continue to give him those opportunities. With Terry down and other guys that have been down, that gives other guys opportunities in terms of Antonio and Chig – and we think we can get even more from Chig.  

On Steve Wilks 

When that opportunity came about, it was a no brainer. It’s something we had talked about and it came into fruition. He had some other obligations with (Appalachian State), where he had some commitments. He wasn’t working in the league this year, so we thought it was a great opportunity. We looked into a number of different possibilities for this role and he was the best fit. … Within the short time he has been here he has aquitted himself well, which I knew he would. He has fit in seamlessly. … Having an extra set of hands is always good and we’re thrilled that he’s here.

item.title: Panthers fire defensive coordinator Ejiro Evero
item.description: At 3-4, Carolina shakes up the defensive side of the ball.
item.content:encoded:
Panthers owner David Tepper had big expectations for his team in 2026. With a 3-4 record after seven games, the team is making some big changes.

The Panthers have announced the terminations of defensive coordinator Ejiro Evero and defensive passing game coordinator Jonathan Cooley.

Moving forward, defensive line coach Todd Wash will serve as defensive coordinator and call the defensive plays.

Outside linebackers coach/run game specialist AC Carter will also coach the defensive line, and secondary coach Renaldo Hill will continue to oversee the defensive backs.

Evero, 45, had worked for the Panthers since 2023, arriving as a member of Frank Reich's staff. Evero remained in place after the hiring of Dave Canales in 2024.

In 2022, Evero was the defensive coordinator of the Broncos. His first job as an NFL position coach came in 2017, when Rams coach Sean McVay hired Evero to serve as safeties coach on McVay's initial staff. Evero was secondary coach and passing game coordinator for the Rams in 2021, which resulted in a Super Bowl win.

Through it all, the Panthers remain tied for first place with the Falcons in the NFC South.

item.title: Chicago Bears at Seattle Seahawks: Keys to a Chicago victory
item.description: Facing a tough road test, our crew shares their keys for Bears victory against Seattle.
item.content:encoded:
In the race for the NFC crown, the Chicago Bears and the Seattle Seahawks each took big swings this week to shore themselves up for the second half of the season.

The Bears obviously made the huge trade for Jeffery Simmons from the Tennessee Titans, while the Seahawks landed Quenton Nelson from the Indianapolis Colts.

Now the Bears and Seahawks face off on Monday Night Football with a lot at stake.

These two teams play in the two best divisions in the conference. The Seahawks are the defending Super Bowl champions. Their record may be 4-3, but they’re hitting their stride, coming off a 20-3 beatdown of the previously undefeated Kansas City Chiefs.

This game should be a great Monday night game, truly a playoff-type atmosphere.

The Bears are eager to show they’re ready to hang with the NFL’s best. The Seahawks want to show they haven’t fallen off from their Super Bowl run.

So we got our crew to weigh in on what it’s going to take for the Bears to go to one of the toughest stadiums in the NFL and come back with the W.

Sam: The biggest defensive test since the Vikings game looms for Caleb and Ben as they go on the road to one of the toughest and loudest stadiums in the league to play in. The Bears will have to take what the defense gives them and grind out long drives to keep JSN off the field. On defense — pressure Sam Darnold and double, heck, triple JSN if you have to. Thieneman over the top, please.

Josh: Caleb needs to level up and display all of his powers, ranging from sack avoidance to completion percentage to explosive plays. Monangai is likely out, and the run game is not as powerful. Defense is just going to have to mitigate damage. Ben needs to be smart and tricky at the same time.

Jeff Berckes: The Seahawks have the best defense by DVOA. The Bears counter with one of the best offenses in the league with Caleb Williams under center. Best on best in a hostile environment – Ben Johnson needs to use that extra rest to his advantage with a game plan that gets the running game back on track to maximize play action. On the other side of the ball… make someone other than JSN beat you. He’s the best receiver in the league and the corners have been rough all year – special attention to him every single play.

Mongo Peanut: The Bears have to contain JSN. He’s the lone offensive weapon that can beat you on a Seattle team still trying to figure out their running game. You won’t keep JSN from catching the ball, but you have to keep him from turning 10-yard catches into 40-yard house calls.

ECD: Offense: Keep as balanced as possible and stay ahead of the chains. It’ll be a classic “immovable object vs unstoppable force” matchup that’ll require strict discipline and situational awareness.

Defense: Do… something. At least bracket JSN as much as possible and find a way to rattle Sam Darnold’s cage. This unit has to play much better on the road than they have in previous weeks.

P.S. Let’s wrap up that trade for a defensive difference-maker soon. (Editor’s note: This piece was mostly written before Thursday’s big trade!)

Special Teams: Let Zavion Thomas cook. He’s recording longer kick returns each week as he gets more opportunities. And keep the FG attempts to a minimum – Seattle is a notorious place to attempt long-range kicks.

What are your keys to the game?

item.title: Miami Dolphins vs. New England Patriots: Three Reasons Why
item.description: Fell deeds awake. Now for wrath, now for ruin, and the red dawn. Forth, Miami Dolphins!
item.content:encoded:
Miami Dolphins fans have enjoyed a post-win week that is always extra enjoyable when it comes against the Jets. But the time has come to put away that excitement and focus on another division opponent: The New England Patriots. For a few seasons, the Pats were a doormat, which they honestly deserve after 2 decades of dominance. But they rebounded last year with a shocking Super Bowl run. That run could maybe be explained by smoke and mirrors (schedule, backup QBs faced, etc.) but make no mistake, the Pats are not a doormat right now. Does this mean the Dolphins have no chance? Absolutely not.

3 REASONS FOR HOPE

THE DOLPHINS ARE BACK HOME

This may seem like a cop-out reason. I have used it in previous home games and in fairness, playing at home is an advantage. But Joe Robbie Hard Rock Stadium has typically been a house of horrors for the Patriots. The Dolphins have hosted the Patriots 61 times in franchise history, including playoffs. The Pats have won in Miami 18 times. That’s a 0.295-win percentage. This isn’t simply a result of the Dolphins being good back in the 70s or when Dan Marino was under center. Since 2000 – the Belichick and Brady era up until the Vrabel era – the Pats have won in Miami 10 times in 26 contests (0.385-win percentage). Brady and the Pats won 9 of those, even including 2008 when Matt Cassel was playing for an injured Brady. In 2000, the Pats finished 5-11. They did not have a losing record again until 2020 when they went 7-9. In that span, the Pats averaged 12.2 wins every season, meaning an average of 3.8 losses per season. You could almost bank on one of those 4 annual losses to be against the Dolphins in Miami. Of course, the circumstances are different this season. The Dolphins are rebuilding and the Pats are coming off a SB run. On the surface, this seems like an easy W for the Pats. But in Miami… the Dolphins have as good a chance as any. The Pats just do not like it there.

THE OFFENSE MAY BE FIGURING THINGS OUT

I don’t want to make too much of the performance against the Jets. It is the Jets after all. But the Dolphins put up 377 yards at 5.5 yards per play against a stingy Jets defense that allows only 4.9 YPP (and that’s after the Dolphins). The Dolphins did it on the road too which is important because the offense has struggled on the road. In 2 home games, the Dolphins average 330 yards per game. In their 3 road games prior to week 7, the Dolphins averaged 247 total yards per game. That average was boosted by a 77-yard garbage time TD against the 49ers. The run game has been the engine driving the offense with Ollie Gordon II taking over for an injured De’Von Achane. He is averaging 4.7 YPC and has scored a TD in each of the last 4 games. Malik Willis is adding to that formula with some designed runs and key scrambles. Willis is 99 yards away from breaking Fiedler’s record for most rushing yards by a QB in a season for the franchise. But Willis also looked like a competent QB passing the ball against the Jets, which was a surprise to me. The Jets have a really good pass defense and given Willis’ struggles in prior games, I was expecting the worst. But he played really well. The Pats defense is decent against the run. They allow 3.9 YPC, which is tied for 12th best. They kept Josh Allen in check in their contest against the Bills with 5 attempts for 4 yards, so they can handle running QBs. But their pass defense is not as daunting, certainly not as good as the Jets statistically. While the Jets allow 6.7 YPA, the Pats are 20th at 7.4 YPA. They have a pressure percentage of 22.2%, which is 18th highest, but they only produce a hurry at a rate of 6%, which is 8th lowest. They blitz at a rate similar to the Jets (36.5 for NE, 36.4 for NYJ). But Miami possibly developed an answer for the blitz against the Jets. Perhaps that carries over. The Pats aren’t a bad defense by any means, but the matchup for Miami isn’t necessarily bad either.

THE PASS RUSH WILL GET HOME THIS WEEK

I have posted the tweets about Chop Robinson and NextGenStats has him tops in the league with a pressure rate of 23.4%. This graph shows that not only is the pressure rate high, but no one gets to the QB as fast as Chop. The issue is the sacks aren’t there. He’s close but that only counts in horseshoes, hand grenades, and nuclear bombs. This week, he’ll get a OT combo of Will Campbell and Morgan Moses. I don’t have access to all the fancy stats i.e. I ain’tagonna pay for it, but from what I can find, Campbell is having a good season. He’s not allowing pressures at a high rate (I’ve seen numbers like 5.6%). RT Morgan Moses on the other hand is parting the Red Sea for defenders, allowing a pressure rate of 14%. He will have his hands full with Robinson. The Pats have a good IOL in terms of pass protection with center Jared Wilson and guards Ben Brown and Alijah Vera-Tucker all ranked top 20 in pass block win rate. But both AVT and Brown were injured and missed time with injuries. Brown could be back, but AVT is now on injured reserve. Something has to give. I dislike making predictions, but I think Chop has his breakout game for this season with at least 2 sacks. BUT EVEN… if the pass rush doesn’t get home, the pressures could create some turnovers. The Pats are tied for the most INTS thrown with 8. In any case, I have a feeling the pass rush finally gets to it this week. It’s only a matter of time before it does.

3 REASONS FOR CONCERN

PASS DEFENSE

I don’t need to keep reminding you about the issues with Miami’s pass defense. Everyone knows about the awful completion percentage allowed. The Jets are a mid-level passing offense but still produced against the Dolphins. The Pats are a top 10 passing offense in both total yards, yards per game, yards per attempt, completion percentage, and passer rating. It’s not a question of whether the Pats passing game will produce, but rather how much they will produce. The Pats acquired AJ Brown from Philly and he will be an issue for whatever CB is facing him. But in the 3 games he has played so far, he only has 9 total catches on 20 targets. He may be due for a breakout game, but thus far, he has been quiet. The Dolphins did well against Garrett Wilson last week. The problem will come from RB Rhamondre Stevenson and – cover your eyes Dolphins – TE Hunter Henry. Stevenson is 3rd in targets with 24 and has 20 catches for 204 yards and a TD. He averages 9.4 yards after catch per reception with an average depth of target (ADOT) of 0.8 yards. He’s essentially getting a 1st down every time he catches the ball. Henry will be another TE thorn in the Dolphins’ flesh unless they get something figured out before Sunday. Henry is 2nd in targets with 31. He has 26 catches for 296 yards and a TD. He averaged 6.6 yards after catch per reception with an ADOT of 6 yards. The Pats spread out their targets fairly evenly, but they’ll most certainly attack the Dolphins with those 2 players. Don’t rule out rookie TE Eli Raridon either. He has 12 catches on 16 targets and 2 TDs this season. His target share has started going up. DeMario Douglas is the top target for the Pats with 34. He has 23 catches, 256 yards and 3 TDs. He works primarily in the slot thus will face rookie Chris Johnson most of the game. Johnson has played well in recent games, but he will be tested. Doubs and Hollins will also be factors. Summing it up, the Pats are going to throw the ball and have success. The real question is how much the Dolphins can limit the damage.

RUN DEFENSE

The Pats’ passing offense will be a problem, but they’ll present a problem on the ground also. The Pats are 8th in total rushing yards (854) and 11th in rushing yards per game (122.0). They are 22nd in rushing TDs with only 5, but they will get move the ball on the ground. The Dolphins are top ten in yards per carry allowed at 3.8 and tied for 4th in rushing TDs allowed with 4. But they are 16th in rushing yards allowed per game at 110.2. They did well against the 49ers and Chiefs – two top 10 teams in yards per game – limiting them to under 100 rushing yards. The Seahawks are the only other defense to keep Kenneth Walker III under 100 yards this season. But in the past 3 games, the Dolphins have allowed subpar rushing attacks to take advantage of them. The Vikings have gained some momentum on the ground after the Dolphins but were not a strong team prior. The Bengals and Jets average less than 100 rushing yards per game on the season, yet were able to gain over 100 yards against Miami. The Bengals only had one game over 100 rushing yards on the season before Miami and the 117 they gained against Miami is their best effort so far. I don’t know what the issue is, but the run defense is slipping. They also have to deal with Drake Maye, who is an effective runner from the QB position. They have only faced a couple of run threats from the QB spot this season. Patrick Mahomes went 1 for 1 yard against the Dolphins. Kyler Murray went 6 for 16, but 3 of those runs were kneeldowns that lost 5 yards. In meaningful game play, he ran 3 times for 21 yards. Maye has 38 attempts for 211 yards and 2 TDs. That’s just over 5 attempts per game. The Dolphins will have to play disciplined run defense against both the RBs and the QB to start plugging the leak.

THE VRABEL FACTOR

The Pats as an organization have not had that much success in Miami. They did win last season however, and one difference is Mike Vrabel. That was his only game against the Dolphins in Miami with New England. But the Dolphins have struggled against Vrabel when he was the coach of the Tennessee Titans. The Dolphins beat him in week 1 of 2018 in that infamous lightning delayed game that took nearly 4 hours. But his Titans squad beat the Dolphins soundly in Tennessee in 2021, ending the Dolphins season and sparking the confrontation between Tua and Flores that ultimately led to Flores’ dismissal. Then Vrabel brought a 4-8 Titans team into Miami on Monday night in 2023 to face the 9-3 Dolphins. Miami was fighting for a playoff spot, division title, and possibly the AFC’s top seed. After a sluggish game, the Dolphins went up 27-13 with 4:34 left in the game. Assuming everything else remained the same, a win here means the Dolphins finish 12-5, the most wins by the franchise since 1990, the first division title since 2008, and a home playoff game against a mid Pittsburgh team led by the Kenny Pickett/Mason Rudolph/Mitchell Trubisky trifecta that very likely would have been the Dolphins’ first playoff win since 2000. 27-13 with 4:34 left. Sigh… let’s leave the past in the past. It’s a small sample size, but I don’t like it. I feel that Vrabel has the Dolphins’ number. Maybe it goes back to his playing days where he had more career sacks against Miami than any other team he faced. Whatever it is, he is a smart HC that knows how to get his team ready to play. Now, one could argue that he faced much softer Miami teams in the past than what Miami will bring under Jeff Hafley. But Vrabel has the experience to win in the margins that Hafley doesn’t have yet.

I SAID WHAT I SAID

ESPN’s Matchup Predictor gives the Pats a 79.7% chance of winning. But as I mentioned last week, in this division, all bets are off. The Dolphins do have some injury issues with Kadyn Proctor and Juju Brents in concussion protocol and may not be available. It’s going to be a tough game for the Dolphins, especially if those two players miss the game. But there have been signs of improvement all season and they finally put it together for a win last week. Can they go a step further and get another win?

*In honor of Sir Patrick Stewart, here is one of the best music themes for a movie ever and in my opinion, the best Star Trek movie. I grew up watching The Next Generation everyday. I always dreamed of exploring the galaxy with Captain Picard and the crew. A big part of my childhood is now gone. Rest in peace, Captain.

item.title: Dallas Cowboys offensive line needs another performance like last week
item.description: How confident are you in the Cowboys offensive line?
item.content:encoded:
The Dallas Cowboys offensive line was the best unit on the field last week against the Philadelphia Eagles. Can they repeat the performance against the Arizona Cardinals? Let’s take a look.

Trench Dashboard

Here are the Cowboys offensive line metrics for the 2026 season so far. 

Pass Block Win Rate – 54% (9th)

Run Block Win Rate – 71% (28th)

Pressure rate allowed – 31% (17th)

Sacks allowed – 7 (1st)

Last three-week trend: Improving nicely 

The Pressure Point

Every opponent will look at the Cowboys offensive line and ask, where can we break it? Here’s what to watch for.

PRESSURE POINT: Do not lose track of Budda Baker

The most dangerous Arizona pass rusher so far is not actually one of its defensive linemen, it’s safety Budda Baker. He leads Arizona with 3.5 sacks, ahead of Josh Sweat and Darius Robinson, who each have two. That immediately tells Dallas something about how Arizona is creating pressure.

Baker has been used selectively as a blitzer. Arizona has found ways to disguise his approach and send him through gaps where offensive linemen are already occupied. One of those plays produced an A-gap sack against Jared Goff. 

If Baker begins close to the line, Dallas has to decide whether he is actually coming after Prescott or simply pretending to blitz before dropping into coverage. That uncertainty is the real danger.

PRESSURE POINT: Josh Sweat versus Terence Steele

Arizona still has one edge defender Dallas cannot ignore. Josh Sweat has only two sacks this season, and his overall production has dropped considerably from 2025. His sacks per 100 pass-rush snaps had fallen from 3.5 last year to 1.6 this year, but he remains Arizona’s most established edge rusher.

The Cardinals themselves described Sweat as their best pass rusher earlier this month, and their depth chart places him at left defensive end, that naturally creates snaps against Terence Steele. 

Tyler Guyton has still not surrendered a sack this season despite allowing 19 pressures, and his 84.6 PFF run-blocking grade ranks fourth among qualifying tackles this year, but Steele has been the less dependable pass protector.

Arizona should therefore move Sweat toward him and see whether it can create a weakness that Philadelphia failed to find. Dallas does not need to completely remove Sweat from the game, it just cannot allow him to turn a quiet season around on Sunday.

Where to attack

Every defensive line has a weakness, here are the Cardinals soft spots and where the Cowboys offensive line should attack. 

GREEN LIGHT: Keep feeding Javonte Williams

There is no reason to complicate this after Dallas finally found its running game against Philadelphia. Now Brian Schottenheimer needs to keep using it.

Arizona has surrendered 884 rushing yards through seven games at 4.6 yards per carry, that’s 126 yards per game which ranks 10th-worst. 

It becomes even more interesting because Arizona could again be missing defensive tackle Walter Nolen III. He missed the Denver game with an ankle injury, and head coach Mike LaFleur said that he was not expecting Nolen to practice much this week, so keep watch on his status as that removes a powerful body from the middle.

That means Dallas should go straight back to Tyler Smith, Cooper Beebe and Tyler Booker where Williams had huge lanes against Philadelphia. There is no reason to move away from that approach this week. 

Arizona defensive lineman Darius Robinson has also struggled against the run. He has a PFF grading of 42.8 against the run, 106th among qualifying interior defensive linemen. That creates another target for Smith and Booker. Double-team Robinson initially, then allow one blocker to move onto a linebacker.

GREEN LIGHT: Make Arizona’s four-man rush beat you

This might be Dallas’ biggest statistical advantage. Arizona’s defense has generated pressure on only 25.5% of opposing dropbacks, which ranks 26th in the NFL and sits below the league average. 

The Cardinals have 15 sacks, 19th in the league, so they have managed to finish some of their pressure opportunities. But they are not consistently forcing quarterbacks to move. Dallas should force Arizona to prove it can win without blitzing. If the Cardinals rush four, send everyone else into a route. Do not automatically keep Jake Ferguson beside the offensive tackle.

Give Prescott five receiving options and make Arizona’s defensive line beat Dallas one-on-one, especially after seeing that Philadelphia could not do it Monday and the Eagles finished without even registering a quarterback hit.

Arizona’s pressure numbers suggest Dallas should trust the offensive line again.

The Chaos Report

Here’s the Arizona Cardinals defensive trends for this season at the defensive line.

Sack Total – 15 (19th)

Pass Rush Win Rate – 52% (14th)

Run Stop Win Rate – 27% (25th)

QB Pressure Rate – 25% (26th)

Last three-week trend: Light pressure, run defense leaking 

Matchup of the week

Terence Steele vs. Josh Sweat

This is the individual matchup Arizona needs to win. The former Eagle has not produced at his normal level this season as Sweat has only two sacks, while Arizona’s overall pressure rate is among the lowest in the league, but Dallas knows all to well what he can do.

Sweat has the speed to attack Steele’s outside shoulder and enough length to prevent the tackle from easily getting his hands into position. Steele does not have to dominate Sweat, he simply cannot allow quick losses and he needs to give Prescott time to attack.

Once those wins start happening and Steele handles his assignment enough times, the Cardinals coaches will need to adjust which in turn helps Steele even more. 

Best Route to Success

The answer here is simple, do exactly what worked in Philadelphia. Run behind Smith and Booker, and let Guyton use his run-blocking ability that currently has him ranked highly on PFF, then make Arizona react.

If the Cardinals bring Baker down toward the line to stop the run, use play-action behind him. If they blitz, throw quickly.

Injury Updates:

Dallas currently has no new injury concerns among its five starting offensive linemen. 

The main Cardinals injury to monitor along the defensive line is Walter Nolen III. Darius Robinson also dealt with a back injury last week but was able to play against Denver. There is some talk of Josh Sweat hitting the trade market before the deadline, but for now expect him to play against Dallas this week.

item.title: Ben Johnson is going for it on fourth down even more than Dan Campbell
item.description: Lions head coach Dan Campbell has earned a reputation as one of the NFL's most aggressive coaches on fourth downs, a reputation that he bolstered on Sunday with a surprising fourth down attempt at his own 24-yard line late in the fourth quarter against the Packers.
item.content:encoded:
Lions head coach Dan Campbell has earned a reputation as one of the NFL’s most aggressive coaches on fourth downs, a reputation that he bolstered on Sunday with a surprising fourth down attempt at his own 24-yard line late in the fourth quarter against the Packers. But it's one of Campbell's former assistants who is going for it on fourth down more than any other coach in the NFL.

Bears head coach Ben Johnson has had his team go for it on fourth down 17 times this season, the most in the NFL. Campbell's Lions, on the other hand, have gone for it on fourth down 13 times, tied for the sixth-most in the NFL.

The Lions have punted twice more than the Bears have, while the Bears have attempted five more field goals than the Lions have. The two teams are similar in all three categories of decisions a coach can make on fourth down, but it's noteworthy that it's Johnson who has gone for it the most in the league so far this season.

Before Campbell's surprising decision on Sunday against the Packers, the most controversial fourth down decision of this NFL season may have been the first fourth down decision Johnson made this season, when the Bears went for it on fourth-and-1 from their own 21-yard line against the Panthers in Week 1. Caleb Williams was stopped for no gain, but the Bears still won the game, and afterward Johnson said the call was part of his overall aggressive approach to trying to field the highest-scoring offense in the NFL.

Confidence in their offense is one thing Campbell and Johnson have in common. They'd rather have the game in the hands of their playmakers than on the feet of their kickers.

item.title: Week 8 Fantasy Football Start/Sit Advice: What to do with Jonathan Taylor amid trade rumors, plus more lineup calls
item.description: Scott Pianowski plays traffic cop, sharing some start/sit advice for your fantasy football lineups in Week 8.
item.content:encoded:
Start-sit decisions can be vexing for even the best of fantasy football managers. If you need help setting your fantasy football lineups, Scott Pianowski offers some assistance with his Week 8 traffic report.

Green Light ✅

WR Garrett Wilson vs. Raiders: The Omar Cooper Jr. breakout is real, but Wilson is a good bet for a rebound here — one week after his sideline displeasure went public against Miami. Most of your downfield routes work against the Raiders, who have allowed a 103.7 passer rating this year, along with 16 touchdown passes. The squeaky-wheel narrative is in play.

TE T.J. Hockenson at Lions: Kyler Murray has struggled to hit intermediate and deep passes all year, but the short passes to Hockenson will be in play Sunday. The Lions have been the worst defense against tight ends by far all season, allowing a touchdown to the position in five of six games.

WR Makai Lemon at Commanders: He finally had a breakout game in Week 7 against Dallas (7-67-1), and the Washington secondary is another favorable matchup. With so many key players hurt from the Philadelphia offense, Lemon is the favorite to command targets Sunday night.

TE Chig Okonkwo vs. Eagles: With Stefon Diggs on the back nine and Terry McLaurin out for the year, the door is open for Okonkwo to become the primary Washington pass-catcher. Okonkwo was involved plenty when we last saw him (7-69-0), and although the Eagles have defended the seam well this year, Okonkwo is a proactive play for Week 8.

RB Braelon Allen vs. Raiders: Even if Breece Hall is able to return this week, the Jets probably can't put the Allen genie back in the bottle. He's been excellent for four straight weeks, and the Raiders are handing out 5.0 YPC.

Yellow Light 😕

RB Jonah Coleman vs. Chiefs: Coleman was easily the best of the Denver backs last week and Sean Payton conceded Coleman has earned a bigger role moving forward. But caveat emptor — the other backs in Denver will play, and Payton is notorious for pumping the air on his players (recall all his Jaylen Waddle optimism this summer). The Chiefs' run defense is also a challenge. Coleman still has the highest upside in this backfield, but the picture might not fully develop in Week 8.

QB Caleb Williams at Seahawks: Williams is usually an auto-start, but the rules are different against an elite defense like Seattle's. The Seahawks are allowing a scant 5.2 YPA and 144.4 passing yards per game, so if your backup QB is in a good spot, it might be prudent to bench Williams.

QB Jared Goff vs. Vikings: Most of what we wrote for Williams would also apply for Goff against Minnesota, though at least Goff sees this opponent twice a year. We also have to consider that the Vikings have feasted on some ideal QB matchups of late — Malik Willis, Tyler Shough, Daniel Jones — so perhaps their statistical profile is slightly misleading.

RB Jordan Mason at Lions: He might have to share with Aaron Jones Sr. (knee) again, and Mason rarely does much in the passing game. But Mason is five years younger than Jones and has more burst as a runner, so we figure Mason can get to 10-plus carries against an ordinary Detroit rushing defense. Consider Mason a lower-end RB2 or a proactive flex play.

Red Light 🚨

RB Jonathan Taylor at Jaguars: The Indianapolis offense is quickly taking on water, and it lost star OG Quenton Nelson this week (traded to Seattle). Jacksonville's defense is outstanding against the run (3.2 YPC) and comes into this game rested. Taylor managers are praying their feature back can sneak a short touchdown, because running lanes will be hard to find.

RB Tyler Allgeier at Cowboys: The Cardinals might be regretting the Allgeier contract, as he's managing just 2.9 YPC and 3.4 yards per touch. Jeremiyah Love might return this week, and even if he doesn't, Bam Knight is probably a better play than Allgeier.

RB Quinshon Judkins at Steelers: The Pittsburgh defense is once again spitting out the run (second-best run defense by DVOA) and Judkins was held to 3.1 YPC in the first meeting. Judkins did save that day with a touchdown and six catches, but the receiving work might not travel here, given that Dylan Sampson has returned.

WR Xavier Worthy at Broncos: The Chiefs are dying for a downfield element in their passing game, but Worthy hasn't been that guy. He's never found much room against the airtight Denver secondary, a meager 4-36-0 log over four career starts.

item.title: Packers’ run game remains abysmal despite win
item.description: The Packers won in spite of their running game yet again.
item.content:encoded:
The Green Bay Packers had a perfect opportunity to get their running game back on track on Thursday. They were facing the Carolina Panthers, who had just allowed 258 rushing yards to the Tampa Bay Buccaneers four days earlier, and they got them on a short week. Josh Jacobs was back — and although mileage will surely vary on whether or not an individual Packers fan thinks that’s a good thing in general, he is clearly the most talented running back on the team’s roster.

So what did the Packers actually do on the ground? They picked up 66 net yards on 26 carries. One of those runs was an end-around to Savion Williams for 18 yards, so the running backs combined for 48 yards on 25 carries, less than two yards per carry on average.

It does not feel like hyperbole to say that this is the worst rushing attack in Packers history, and it may well be the worst in NFL history. The fact that the Packers threw the ball on 3rd and 2 late in the game to try to run out the clock should come as no surprise, because this offense has no choice but to run through Jordan Love.

And Love played well once again on Thursday night, generally getting the ball out quickly and accurately. Love had just one mistake — a terrible decision on an interception towards the end zone early in the fourth quarter — but otherwise he put up a great performance. 30 of 41 for 288 yards and three touchdowns will get the job done most days, and it certainly did against the Panthers on Sunday.

The Packers still made their share of mistakes. Two fumbles, including one on the opening kickoff, could have been a death sentence against a better team. There were still drops, though Matthew Golden made up for one in the end zone with a touchdown on the very next play. But the penalty issues were better, and maybe there’s something to build on here.

It just isn’t the running game.

Game recap: 5 takeaways from Packers’ victory over Panthers | Packers.com
While the offense still has major issues to iron out, the defense stifled Carolina for much of the game, getting some big 4th down stops and posting six sacks, one each from six different players.

Christian Watson’s return from hospital leaves Packers teammates stunned | Packers Wire
Watson left the game in the first half and got checked out at a local hospital, but he returned in an ambulance after halftime and made a clutch catch on 3rd-and-2 to all but seal the game.

Packers Report Card: Big Win Over Panthers Comes With Two F’s | SI.com
The run game, as expected, gets a failure, but so does the special teams, thanks to another missed PAT by Trey Smack and the fumble by Coleman Owen on the opening kick.

Packers’ Josh Jacobs: TD celebration was ode to gospel song, not mocking arrest | ESPN
I’m sorry, when you have more than 20 carries and fewer than 40 yards, it’s tough to celebrate too much at all. But the lack of awareness by Jacobs for how his “handcuffs” celebration would be perceived is just another example of poor judgment on his part.

Here’s a good recap on just how badly the Packers missed their chance to get the run game going again:

Patrick Stewart, legendary actor of ‘Star Trek’ and ‘X-Men’ fame, dies at 86 | AP.com
No funny link tonight, just a sad one: one of the iconic actors of the last several decades, and a genuinely excellent human being, passed away this week. Shaka, when the walls fell.

item.title: Which NFL Week 8 game are you most looking forward to?
item.description: Other than the Detroit Lions’ matchup against the Minnesota Vikings, which Week 8 game are you most looking forward to?
item.content:encoded:
I think this every year, but the 2026 NFL season feels like it is flying by. Despite October almost being over, it feels like everything just got underway a few weeks ago. With that said, I doubt many of the players feel that way. After all, the regular season is a grind that players and coaches often refer to as a marathon, as opposed to an all-out sprint. Filled with peaks and valleys, veteran teams learn not to ride the waves. Just try your best to keep stacking wins as you head into the holiday months.

That is where we find the Detroit Lions in their Week 8 matchup against the Minnesota Vikings. After securing their first divisional win against the Green Bay Packers in Week 7, they will be looking to improve to 2-0 in the division, and 5-2 overall on the year. If you are looking for a fresh take on that game, be sure to check out Anthony Balaj’s three key matchups article.

I know a lot of fans enjoy the Lions being in primetime windows, or even the 4 p.m. ET slot like they were against Green Bay. Still, there is something nice about the Lions’ game against Minnesota being at 1 p.m. ET. If you are at home, you can simply flip the channel to the next game. For me, I have about a 15-minute drive before I can be on my couch for the afternoon slate of games. That brings us to our question of the day—which game other than the Lions vs. Vikings are you most looking forward to in Week 8?

My answer: I am going with the “Monday Night Football” game between the Chicago Bears and the defending Super Bowl Champion Seattle Seahawks. The Bears are riding high right now, currently firmly in the mix for what is looking like it will be an ultra-competitive NFC North race. Seattle got out of the gates a bit slow, but with that defense, it’s tough to ever count them out.

What about you? Which game other than the Lions are you most looking forward to in Week 8? Let us know in the comments below.

item.title: Browns vs. Steelers Week 8 picks: Everyone seems to be on the Pittsburgh bandwagon
item.description: The Browns have fought their way to a 5-2 record and beaten the Steelers once, but very few people think Cleveland will win the re-match.
item.content:encoded:
The Cleveland Browns take on the Pittsburgh Steelers this Sunday. Both teams enter with the same record, but Cleveland has the division edge after beating Pittsburgh on Thursday Night Football earlier this season. The Steelers are undefeated at home, so are they looking to give medicine back to the Browns?

Here is what the national media is saying about the Week 8 game between the Browns and Steelers:

NFL.com (Various)

Why Brooke picked the Steelers: In their first meeting, the Browns’ defense controlled the line of scrimmage, sacking Aaron Rodgers five times while piling up 10 total QB hits and keeping the veteran signal-caller all out of sorts. Things have turned a corner for the Steelers’ offense in the last three weeks, with Rodgers playing in rhythm, limiting the giveaways and accurately finding his targets — though there’s still a lot of pressure on rookie right tackle Max Iheanachor, who allowed two sacks and seven pressures (per NGS) against the Browns in Week 4. Everything about the 42-year-old quarterback’s play has trended upward since their last meeting, and the rushing attack should flex its muscle more this time around with the return of Rico Dowdle. The Browns have rightfully earned their place at the top of the division through two months, but how long can they end up on the winning side of close games? We’ve seen this type of playing-with-fire approach before, and it rarely lasts. That said, watching this team get meaningful contributions from young players (Denzel Boston, KC Concepcion, Spencer Fano, Carson Schwesinger) has been enjoyable and should keep Cleveland competitive should they maintain that level. But this Sunday, playing the steadily improving, veteran-laden Steelers within confines of Acrisure Stadium could be the Browns’ toughest matchup to date. Pittsburgh improves to 4-0 at home and takes over first place in the AFC North at midseason.

CBS Sports (Pete Prisco) – Steelers 24, Browns 20

This is a big game for the division lead in the AFC North. The Browns beat the Steelers earlier this year, but this will be a bigger challenge on the road. They are also playing consecutive road games, which will be a challenge. Look for Aaron Rodgers to play well as the Steelers take it.

CBS Sports (John Breech) – Browns 23, Steelers 20

The Browns have already beaten the Steelers once this season, and if they win this game, that would give them their first season sweep of Pittsburgh since 1988. That’s right, it has somehow been 38 years since the Browns have swept the Steelers. The NFL should have flexed this game to Sunday night and asked everyone at the stadium to dress up like their favorite character from 1988. I would have definitely been John McClane from Die Hard, or maybe AC Slater. You know what? I’m not sure and we don’t have time to talk about this. … (read more on CBS)

Sporting News (Vinnie Iyer) – Steelers 24, Browns 20

The Browns have all their five wins thanks to Deshaun Watson snatching victory from the jaws of defeat late in the fourth quarter. That’s a feel-good development for rookie coach Todd Monken, but not sustainable as a first-place team. Aaron Rodgers is feeling it since the last Cleveland matchup and will outduel Watson with superior weapons.

Sporting News (Bill Bender) – Steelers 23, Browns 16

The Browns are 5-1 in one-score games – and their last six games have been decided by six points or less. Cleveland beat Pittsburgh in the first matchup, too. This time, Pittsburgh will build off the running game. The Steelers are 3-0 S/U at home, and Aaron Rodgers has a 101.6 passer rating.

item.title: Fantasy Football Week 8 Fades & Busts: Leave the Broncos in the stable
item.description: Fantasy football analyst Matt Okada highlights key players to fade in Week 8.
item.content:encoded:
Welcome to the eighth of 17 weekly articles spotlighting the fantasy fades of the week! I am your host, Matt Okada, and I'll be bringing you half a dozen potential busts each and every Friday, from now until the fantasy championships.

As a note, just because a player earns a "fade" or "bust" designation doesn't automatically mean they should be benched — it depends on the rest of your roster or the options on your waiver wire. But you can expect them to fall short of expectations (when I get them right). I include a "What to Do" section for every player to help with that.

Without further ado, here is my list for Week 8 of the 2026 season.

Bo Nix, QB, Broncos vs. Chiefs

With three quarterbacks typically in the starter conversation on bye, and following a massive fantasy performance against the Cardinals, Bo Nix might be on a lot of streaming radars for Week 8.

Turn the radar off.

Nix scored 12.2 of his 26.18 fantasy points on an absurd 62-yard rushing touchdown that will never happen again in his career. Meanwhile, as a passer, he completed just 51.7% of his passes for 222 yards and one TD — with 52 yards and the TD coming on a pass behind the line of scrimmage to RJ Harvey that went for 60 yards after the catch. Nix had scored fewer than 14 fantasy points in each of the previous three weeks and still only has one game with multiple touchdown passes all season.

And while Arizona is one of the softest quarterback matchups in the league, Kansas City has been among the toughest, allowing 13.03 points per game to the position, third-fewest behind the Seahawks and Vikings. They've only allowed 14+ points to one QB all season (Kirk Cousins in Week 4), and the list of previous busts includes Nix himself, who scored just 5.44 in Week 1 with 131 passing yards, one TD, an INT and a fumble lost. This has all the makings of an ugly, defensive divisional battle in Denver — one which the Broncos will only win by controlling the clock with the ground game and stifling Patrick Mahomes. Don't chase the points with Nix.

What to do ❓ Nix isn't just a bad QB1 play ... he falls to the very fringe of QB2 range in this matchup. Do not start him outside of desperate situations in leagues with multiple starting quarterbacks.

J.K. Dobbins, RB, Broncos vs. Chiefs

Alright, so if we're sitting Nix while Denver leans on the run game, we should start J.K. Dobbins, right? Right?! Sorry, but no. I recognize that Dobbins has scored a touchdown in three straight games and that running back is a shallow position getting shallower by the day. But he might be one of the bigger traps in fantasy for Week 8 ... and the rest of the season. In the five games without rookie Jonah Coleman this season, Dobbins has averaged a strong 16 opportunities, but just 52.2 scrimmage yards and 8.4 fantasy points per game. That includes a 3.6-point showing against these Chiefs in Week 1.

Then in the two games that Coleman has been active — Week 2 and 7 — Dobbins has totaled just 16 opportunities and 59 scrimmage yards. In Coleman's return to action last Sunday, Dobbins played just 21.4% of the snaps, fewer than RJ Harvey (25.0%) and less than half of Coleman's share (50.0%). It's clear Denver wants to make Coleman its RB1 when healthy, which relegates Dobbins to touchdown-dependent, change-of-pace back. Even the TD he scored last week only got him up to 8.3 fantasy points. And the Chiefs are a particularly bad matchup for Dobbins and his narrow path to relevance: they've allowed the fifth-fewest rushing yards per game to running backs (73.7) and the second-lowest red-zone touchdown rate in the league (26.7%).

The floor is two or three fantasy points and the ceiling for Dobbins is an unlikely touchdown ... to narrowly squeak into RB2 territory. 

What to do ❓ Dobbins shouldn't be anywhere close to starting lineups, outside of a low-upside FLEX consideration in extremely deep leagues. And if things go as expected this Sunday, he'll be a drop candidate by the time the weekend's over.

TreVeyon Henderson, RB, Patriots at Dolphins

If you're one of the many fantasy managers who drafted TreVeyon Henderson in the middle rounds, hoping he would take over the New England backfield and become a strong RB2, you might be staring at the bright green Miami matchup this weekend with your very last dregs of hope and optimism. I don't blame you, but you simply cannot play Henderson, even in what should be a favorable game script.

Over the last five weeks, Henderson has totaled 17.7 fantasy points. For the math-averse, that's 3.5 points per game. He's logged single-digit touches in four of those five games and had just 42 rushing yards in the one game with volume. And it's not just Rhamondre Stevenson keeping him from relevance. Former undrafted free agent Corey Kiner has had more touches (22) and scrimmage yards (129) than Henderson (18 and 101) over the past three weeks. As a result, Henderson no longer possesses any meaningful role in the Patriots offense: not the early-down role, the third-down role, the short-yardage role, the receiving role, the goal-line role or even the salt-the-game-away role. He's essentially Dobbins with a slightly better chance at a breakaway play, but less occasional touchdown upside.

Whatever you thought of him when you drafted him, adjust your expectations to the range of Mike Washington Jr. or Kimani Vidal. Until something changes in New England — which I don't foresee any time soon — Henderson is a bench asset at best.

What to do ❓ Like Dobbins, Henderson shouldn't be in any starting lineups this weekend, unless you play in a 16-team league and have zero running back depth.

Rome Odunze, WR, Bears at Seahawks

Unfortunately for those who selected Rome Odunze in the middle rounds, the Bears wide receiver has shown shockingly little upside through seven weeks. He had one outing with 94 yards, back in Week 4, but has averaged just 3.4 receptions per game and does not have a single touchdown all season. Both Luther Burden III and Colston Loveland have stepped up since Caleb Williams' return, and the run game remains the crux of the offense, leaving Odunze with a relatively small share of a relatively small pie. He is — please sit down before continuing — the WR54 in half-PPR points per game, below Ryan Flournoy and Jaylin Noel.

And while there are small signs that he could improve down the stretch, that improvement is unlikely to start this Monday night against Seattle. The Seahawks have allowed the fewest fantasy points per game to wideouts this year (16.46), while surrendering a league-low 91.7 receiving yards per game to the position. They've allowed the league's lowest explosive pass rate, at just 8.4%, more than two points lower than the 49ers in second place (10.7%) and almost half the league average (15.1%). The only wideouts to score double-digit fantasy points against this defense were Mike Evans and Terry McLaurin, who both saw 9+ targets and scored a touchdown.

Odunze is not a great bet for either against Seattle, so the breakout is very likely to be delayed another week (if it comes at all in 2026).

What to do ❓ Odunze is outside WR3 range in Week 8, so the only way he should crack lineups is as a volatile FLEX play. Expect single-digit fantasy points once again.

Ladd McConkey, WR, Chargers at Rams

We're continuing this week's trend of players drafted high enough to induce starting-lineup stubbornness eight weeks into the season. Ladd McConkey had a strong Week 1 — five catches for 82 yards, a TD and 16.7 fantasy points — but between injuries and underperformance for the entire Chargers offense, he's done nothing since. He has a sub-20% target rate on his routes run and even if we stick to just the first three weeks, before his foot injury aggravation and concussion, McConkey trailed both Quentin Johnston (19.8%) and Tre' Harris (18.6%) in target share (at just 17.4%). And, of course, Los Angeles currently ranks 27th in passing yards per game (190.2) and 29th in passing touchdowns per game (0.8), so none of the receivers in this corps have done anything consistent for fantasy. McConkey should be healthy after the bye, but he's returning for a matchup with the Rams, who should get corner Trent McDuffie back this week as well.

The other Los Angeles team has allowed the seventh-fewest fantasy points per game to wide receivers and, in particular, the second-fewest yards per game and third-fewest yards per target on downfield throws, where McConkey has seen the majority of his targets. It's not impossible the Chargers figured something out over their bye, but until we see it on the field, you can't trust McConkey or this passing attack in general, particularly against the Rams' secondary.

What to do ❓ McConkey is a low-end WR3 with a wide range of outcomes this week, so you can play him in a pinch, but I'd try to avoid it. 

Jake Ferguson, TE, Cowboys vs. Cardinals

It's an even shallower-than-normal week for tight ends with George Kittle, Isaiah Likely and a couple of fringe TE1s on bye this week, so Jake Ferguson will pop up as a streaming candidate.

It's a "No" from me, dawg.

He had three touchdowns in Weeks 2 and 3 combined and has ridden that small spike of fantasy value the rest of the season. But the Cowboys tight end has fewer than four catches and fewer than 25 receiving yards in six of seven games this season, and has scored fewer than four fantasy points in four straight games. That includes a complete goose egg last Monday night against the Eagles. Ferguson has a 9.4% target share on the season and has just one "target" in the red zone since Week 4 (it was essentially a throwaway into the back of the defender covering Ferguson on a long scramble by Dak Prescott). Even in a decent matchup with the Cardinals, Ferguson is nothing more than a low-upside dart throw at a touchdown on a team that prefers Javonte Williams in scoring range and either CeeDee Lamb or George Pickens when they do throw.

You're better off taking a shot on one of the Rams tight ends or picking up Chig Okonkwo (whom I actually love moving forward).

What to do ❓ Ferguson is outside the top 25 at tight end, so you're not playing him in any reasonable context. Scour the waiver wire for a streaming option, if you must.
